utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-96-21-Abis, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Mucic, Hazim Delic, and Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: At the beginning, I think it is proper to tender an apology to the participants in this case for the lateness in the taking of our positions on the Bench. It was due for good personal reasons. Thank you very much. Now, can the appellants hear me? Mr. Mucic? THE APPELLANT MUCIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Delic? And Mr. Landzo? THE APPELLANT LANDZO: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now we will take the appearances. First counsel for the appellants. Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Tom Kuzmanovic and Howard Morrison here on behalf of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Delic counsel for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, I am Salih Karabdic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: -- my colleague Thomas Moran, from Houston. We represent Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Cynthia Sinatra, and along with my esteemed counsel, Professor Peter Murphy, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And now we move to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Prosecution Norman Farrell, Ms. Helen Brady, Mr. Anthony Carmona and with us is Mr. Wolfgang Sakulin who is our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I have received this morning a written communication from counsel for the appellants. The Bench has also been supplied with a copy. Let me ask Mr. Hocking for a copy. Have you got a copy, Mr. Hocking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The speaking order indicated is agreeable to us subject to what the Prosecution has to say. I understand that Mr. Murphy will speak on jurisdictional issues. Mr. Moran will speak on jurisdictional issues relating to cumulative sentencing. Mr. Kuzmanovic will speak on Fifth Amendment issues. That, I believe, has to do with the right of silence. And individual issues will then be dealt with by Mr. Moran and Ms. Sinatra. Have you -- has the Prosecution got a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, we haven't seen the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You will be given a copy now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It has to do with the speaking order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The most important thing is that -- well, an important thing, I believe, is that you will, together, confine yourself within the time limits prescribed by the Court. So now we will hear Mr. Murphy on jurisdictional issues concerning cumulative sentences. Yes. You may now begin. Are you ready, Mr. Murphy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, before I come to address the provisions of the Statute of the Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I would, if I may, like to make one observation that I think really goes to the heart of this issue which has been brought before the Appeals Chamber and which shows that this is not a semantic or academic question but one that goes to the very heart of the sentencing procedure in the Tribunal. I would submit that in all civilised jurisdictions, it is a basic principle of sentencing that the sentence should be imposed based upon information available at the time when sentence is passed. This is just a statement of general principle. In the present case, Your Honours, as you know, the first sentencing Chamber, the Trial Chamber, passed sentence on these accused in November of 1998, and it was not until October of 2001 that the second Trial Chamber made its ruling which is the subject of the present appeal. Essentially, what we say is even if one leaves aside the provisions of the Statute and the provisions of the Rules, good sentencing procedure would have demanded that the sentence be passed with full information about the present condition of these accused, as well, of course, as the history, as contained in the record, developed by the Trial Chamber, and in this case that was not done, despite the fact that almost three years had elapsed between the two sentences. Now, when one comes to look at the law, I would respectfully submit that what one finds is this: that this good standard sentencing practice has been enshrined in the Statute of the Tribunal and it's been enshrined in the Rules, as one would expect it to be. The combined effect of Article 24(2) of the Statute and Rule 101(B) of the Rules is to require a sentencing Chamber to have regard to certain matters. Your Honours are quite familiar with these provisions. They're set out in our brief. I need not read them to you. But of course, one of the things that must be assessed is the individual circumstances of the accused. Now, looking at the procedural history of this case, what do we see? We see that the Appeals Chamber, the first Appeals Chamber, when considering this matter, clearly was not concerned with any detailed argument from counsel or a consideration of the law regarding its powers. But when it made the order to refer the case to a new sentencing Chamber, what the Appeals Chamber called a reconstituted Trial Chamber, it did so with what the second Trial Chamber interpreted as being a very narrow mandate, namely, to consider only the issue of whether some adjustment of sentence should be made because of the fact that certain cumulative charges had been dismissed, and my learned friend Ms. Sinatra will deal with the implications of that as a matter of the Court's discretion. But the argument that I advance, which will be -- I do, really, on behalf of both Mr. Landzo and Mr. Mucic. Mr. Delic has a slightly different argument on this point. The argument that we advance is simply this: that the Appeals Chamber certainly had the power to cause the issue of sentence to be considered by a second Trial Chamber. That could have been done, but we submit that it must have been done under Rule 117, thereby giving the appellants what is referred to in the Rule as a new trial according to law. And we submit that when the Rule speaks of a new trial according to law -- Your Honour, I'm going to pause just so that I can have a clear sight of the Bench. When the Rule speaks of a new trial according to law, we submit that that means a new trial which takes into account the relevant provisions of the Statute, the Rules, and the law from other sources that this Tribunal may consider. The fact is that that was not done. A new trial need not have been a protracted affair. Nobody suggests that the second sentencing Chamber had to reopen the issues which had been already concluded by the first Trial Chamber or the first Appeals Chamber as regards conviction, as regards the underlying facts of the case, or even to reopen the various issues of mitigation or aggravation that were placed before the first Trial Chamber. Those had all been considered. But what the appellants, in our submission, were entitled to was to place before the Court such facts as might bear on the question of their individual circumstances not in November 1998 but in October 2001, because in our respectful submission, those circumstances had necessarily changed in that period of almost three years. Your Honours, in a sense, the issue in this case comes down to this: Will the Statute and the Rules be strictly applied or will the Court, as invited to by the Prosecution, say, "Well, we need to have an inherent power because it's necessary to make the appeal process work, and that can only be done by the Appeals Chamber having certain inherent powers to regulate the conduct of its own affairs." Now, Your Honours, we do not dispute that the Appeals Chamber, like any other court, has certain inherent powers. Clearly, when we're talking about formal matters, such as correcting an error in the record, when we're talking about dealing with a contempt in the face of the Court, these are well-recognised powers. Nobody disputes that the Appeals Chamber could exercise those powers. This is a different case. The Prosecution argues that the Appeals Chamber has some kind of inherent power to increase its own jurisdiction, to increase its own powers to an extent not provided for either in the Statute or the Rules. They call this a purposive or a theological interpretation. But Your Honours, whatever name one gives to it, the fact is that this is a criminal court, that the Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chambers are creatures of Statute, and that the statutory provision in this case dealing with the powers of the Court, Article 25(2), is not in any way grammatically ambiguous, and we submit that it should be interpreted strictly and it should be interpreted strictly in favour of the accused. The other point that I should address is that the Prosecution cites the Tadic case as being authority for the course of action taken by the first Trial Chamber in this case. Your Honours, we have set out in our brief something of the detailed history of the Tadic case from which it is quite clear that when Mr. Tadic was held to be guilty of further offences because of the Appeals Chamber's ruling and the sentence was sent back to a new Trial Chamber partly comprised of the original Judges, partly not, that Trial Chamber did exactly what the appellants in this case contend should have been done. They not only looked at the record of the trial, they also obtained up-to-date information about Tadic from the United Nations Detention Unit, and they allowed Tadic to make a statement as provided by Rule 100. The appellants in this case ask the Trial Chamber, second Trial Chamber, to permit that course of action also, and the Trial Chamber interpreted the Appeals Chamber's order as being that that was not permissible, that no evidence was required, and that the only issue was the issue of an adjustment of sentence. Your Honours, it's our submission that simply put, the Trial Chamber have no jurisdiction to sentence the appellants, the second Trial Chamber, because the order of the first Appeals Chamber exceeded the powers that the Appeals Chamber has under Article 24(2) and 101(B). The Appeals Chamber could have achieved its object by ordering a new trial according to law on the limited issue of sentence, but it did not do so. Lastly, the Prosecution contends while there was no prejudice to the appellants through this because all the relevant matters had been considered by the first sentencing Chamber. Your Honours, all the matters which were required by the Rule were not considered by the first sentencing Chamber because clearly, almost three years later, they were not then available. And we say that the present position is that these appellants were not properly sentenced because the second sentencing Chamber lacked jurisdiction to do so. Do Your Honours have any questions on these submissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, your principal argument as to why this was an improper procedure is that you were denied the opportunity of presenting up-to-date evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Of course the Appeals Chamber was being asked by you to reduce your client's sentence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And if it had gone ahead and upheld your appeal, it would have then been open to the Appeals Chamber, the first Appeals Chamber, to impose a fresh sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you never tendered any evidence before that Appeals Chamber for that purpose, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. The Prosecution drew attention to that fact, but as the Prosecution put it in their brief, the proceedings before the Appeals Chamber were not a de novo rehearing of the issue of sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's not the point that I have asked you about. You asked the Appeals Chamber to upset the sentence because it was manifestly excessive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Which would have required the Appeals Chamber, if it had decided to do so itself, to have resentenced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that would have permitted you to have put forward your up-to-date evidence, wouldn't it? That is the usual way these things are done in appellate courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before an Appellate Court, my understanding is that the Appeals Chamber was looking at the record as developed by the first Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But in order to resentence him, it would have been open to you to have brought the evidence up to date. Now, that can be answered yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It would have been open to us, Your Honour, to offer that evidence to the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you didn't do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: We did not do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got any reason for not doing so, other than your misguided belief that it was -- that it only be available on a de novo hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue on which we invited the Appeals Chamber to rule was one of law based upon the wording of Article 25(2). We had to bring to the Appeals Chamber's attention something that had gone wrong in the first Trial Chamber relating to the sentence. Now, for that purpose, the record before the Trial Chamber was plainly relevant, but I would anticipate that if I had stood before Your Honour on that occasion and said we have up-to-date information, Your Honour might well have said to me, "How does that bear on whether or not the sentence was excessive when imposed by the first Trial Chamber which is the subject of the appeal?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's because I've been on sitting on one or other type of Appeals Chamber for many years, but I can assure you I never would have had the audacity to say that. It is done every day in appellate criminal courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not familiar with the practice in Your Honour's jurisdiction. I do know that in the jurisdiction in which I began my practice, the Court of Appeals might possibly have entertained up-to-date information, but they would be much more likely to require a Trial Chamber or a Trial Court to do so. On the issue before the Appeals Chamber would be one of law, namely, did the Judge of first instance make a decision that was manifestly excessive or did the Judge get it right within the discretionary framework available? And as I understand it, Your Honour, that was the issue we brought before the first Appeals Chamber. Your Honour, if I may add one more thing to that. Even if we had brought evidence forward at that time and the Appeals Chamber had made the same order notwithstanding, namely that we have to refer it back to a second Trial Chamber, we would still have contended that the state of affairs would have to be examined at the date of the second sentence and not at the date even of the -- of the judgement in the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The only problem is you didn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I don't know whether the issue was raised Your Honour, at that time, and I think the possible referral back to a second Trial Chamber, as far as I recall, was not expressly adverted to during that appeal. Unless the Bench has any other questions, I will defer to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, would you take a question from Judge Gunawardana.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: You said that the Appeals Chamber referred the case to the second Trial Chamber on the basis that they should look into the effect of the acquittal on the cumulative charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Now, thereby this Court [indiscernible] refers to the Appeals Chamber is limited. Then at the state that you said there were changes that took place just after the first Appeals Chamber, the first conviction in the first Trial Chamber and the hearing before the second Trial Chamber, but what were the changes you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Because you didn't lead any evidence, the only issue before the second Trial Chamber -- the issue before second Appeal -- Trial Chamber was the issue to consider the effect of the cumulative charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the point of the -- of any new evidence or of perhaps getting a report from the United Nations Detention Unit would be to satisfy the requirement which is laid down by Article 24(2) and Rule 101(B) that the individual circumstances of the accused be taken into account. And, Your Honour, we can't say -- I'm not saying that that would necessarily have made a difference, because we don't know, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: No. The point is you did not make any de novo to lead any evidence of making sure the new circumstances. So all the circumstances that prevailed before the first -- second Trial Chamber were the same facts as it was before the first Trial Chamber except for the fact of the cumulative charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes. The -- the circumstances of the cumulative charges, of course, were something that the first Appeals Chamber said should be considered, and we did address that before the second Trial Chamber. But that was a matter which could have been considered, in any event, if the Appeals Chamber had ordered a new trial under Rule 117. But in addition to that, we say that the Rules and the Statute entitle the accused to have the opportunity of putting forward to the sentencing tribunal such facts as they might be. And I take Your Honour's point that it's possible these facts would not have been regarded by the Court as significant, but nonetheless, the appellants had the -- should have had the opportunity to present them, and the accused should have been given the opportunity to make a sentence -- a statement, rather, on sentence under Rule 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: But as my brother pointed out, Judge Hunt, that you made no effort to do such thing at the hearing of the second appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- there was a motion made to the second Trial Chamber on behalf of Mr. Delic. Before any other motions could be made, there was a ruling on that motion, and the second Trial Chamber declined to entertain any further evidence. So we were, in fact, precluded from introducing such evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Well, the second Trial Chamber made the order on the facts that were available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't quite hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: So the second Trial Chamber made the order in regard to sentence on the facts that were available to them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they did, except for this: that the Trial Chamber specifically said that it wasn't going to consider the facts. I think we set out an extract from the Court's ruling in our brief, and what the Trial Chamber said was, We have been instructed by the Appeals Chamber only to consider one issue," and that issue was given that these are proper sentences, should any adjustment be made to the sentences because of the dismissal of the cumulative charges? At least was true in Mr. Landzo's case. I know in Mr. Mucic's case there was an additional issue, but the basic issue of jurisdiction was in that one order. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Meron now. Are you still up standing, Mr. Murphy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Murphy, let me clarify one point with you, if I may. You do accept that the Appeals Chamber had the authority itself to resentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And is it your position that the Appeals Chamber would have had to take into account mitigating evidence not available during the first trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we might have offered that evidence, but as I said in response to Judge Hunt, our understanding of the issue that is required to be before an Appeals Chamber by Article 25 is whether or not the Trial Chamber made an error because it imposed a manifestly excessive sentence, and that would have to be looked at in the light of the record as developed at that time. Now, if the Appeals Chamber decided, after argument on that point, to revise the sentence, of course we have no problem with that. That's within the powers of the Chamber. If they had ordered a new Chamber to consider the record and conduct a new trial on that issue, we have no problem with that. All we're saying is that what cannot be done is that a discrete issue, in a vacuum, without any reference to the record or the new facts, can be referred to a Trial Chamber in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, just one small question from me, if you don't mind. I ought to have been clearer than I am, having read the pleadings and listened to your arguments, but I think it prudent to ask you to clarify just one point for me, and that is to say this: Is it your case that the new Trial Chamber misconstrued the decision of the Appeals Chamber, or is it your case that the new Trial Chamber correctly construed the decision of the Appeals Chamber? I'm referring to what you have referred to as a narrow construction --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- placed by the new Trial Chamber on the remit ordered by the Appeals Chamber. In one case, you would be directly attacking the jurisdiction of the new Trial Chamber; in the other case, you would be attacking it also, but indirectly, in the sense that your real thrust would be against the vires of the decision of the Appeals Chamber itself. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would say that the Appeals Chamber itself had no power to refer the matter in the way it did. I think we would submit that the second Trial Chamber was certainly entitled to construe the Appeals Chamber's order in the way it did, but our argument is that if the Appeals Chamber did not have power to make that order, then it would follow that the second sentencing Trial Chamber had no jurisdiction to pass sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you confirm one other aspect for me? That is to say that you are not contending on the basis that this Appeals Chamber, this Bench, has a power to hear an appeal from the decision of the previous Bench of the Appeals Chamber but that it has a power of reconsideration? Is that your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honours have the power to affirm, reverse, or revise any decisions taken by the Trial Chambers. And the decisions taken by the Trial Chamber in this case, as far as Landzo is concerned, were to hold -- firstly to hold that they had jurisdiction to pass sentence. That was an issue that we had raised with the Trial Chamber by means of a motion. And then, of course, the sentencing order itself made by the Trial Chamber, Your Honours have power to deal with that order, to hear an appeal from that order, under Article 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're not asking us, then, to hear an appeal from the previous decision of another Bench of this same Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The issue here is whether or not the -- the only jurisdiction I believe Your Honours have is to consider an appeal from the decision of the second sentencing Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The new Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question: Mr. Landzo appealed against his conviction in respect of the death of Gotovac, but I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think Your Honour is thinking of Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Delic was also convicted in respect of the death of Gotovac; that is true. But was Landzo also convicted in respect of that death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, he was, but that was not the subject of an appeal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But did the Appeals Chamber dismiss an appeal on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No. The Appeals Chamber -- the only action that the Appeals Chamber took in Mr. Landzo's case was to dismiss certain cumulative charges. They did not allow an appeal against a conviction on the merits of any one of the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the death of Gotovac, Mr. Landzo had been sentenced to 20 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Fifteen, I think, Your Honour. Fifteen. The maximum sentence Mr. Landzo received on any one count was 15 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Fifteen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, and all the sentences in his case were ordered to run concurrently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. My reading was inadequate on that point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've confused me, I'm afraid, Mr. Murphy. You say you are not arguing that the decision of the Appeals Chamber to send a limited issue to a Trial Chamber was ultravires so far as the Appeals Chamber is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do argue that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, you do? Well, then, your answer to Judge Shahabuddeen surely would be: Yes, you are arguing that the first Appeals Chamber had no power to do what it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You described it as per curiam, apart from some of the more polite descriptions, which your colleagues don't seem to share. But nevertheless, it is part of your case: The first Appeals Chamber had no power to do what it did?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. But His Honour -- I understood His Honour's question to be whether we were appealing against -- trying to appeal against the order of the first Trial Chamber or the order of the first -- of the second -- the first Appeals Chamber or the order of the second Trial Chamber, and of course clearly we must appeal against the order of the Trial Chamber under Article 25. I apologise if I misled the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then we turn to Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I think I may be able to clear up some of the confusion here. Mr. Delic is asking the Appeals Chamber to reconsider the analysis in the Gotovac murder case based on its decision in Kupreskic -- not Gotovac. Milosevic. And because of that -- I think that's the confusion, Your Honour. On the issue of the jurisdiction of the Trial Chamber, Delic takes a slightly different view than that taken by Mucic and Landzo. What we are doing is looking to the substance of what this Chamber did in the initial appeal rather than the form that it did it in. It's our position that the Statute gives the Chamber the authority to do three things, the jurisdiction to do three things: It can affirm, reverse, or revise the judgement of the Trial Chamber. In this case, as applied to Delic, what the Appeals Chamber did was vacate the sentence and remand it to a Trial Chamber for reconsideration of sentence. Now, it was done in terms of an adjustment and reconsider, but basically what the Appeal Chamber did was remand this case down to a Trial Chamber. Maybe at this point, Judge Hunt, may I try and answer our view on your question to Mr. Murphy on presentation of evidence to the Appeals Chamber in the first appeal. We appealed against sentence that it was manifestly unjust. The Appeals Chamber, looking at the record set forth in front of the Trial Chamber, found that it was not manifestly excessive but vacated the sentence because of the cumulative convictions and the appellate reversal as to count 1 of the indictment, the murder count, and sent it back down. So the issue of whether the sentence, the initial sentence, was manifestly excessive was not remanded to the Trial Chamber. The issue of whether or not we should have presented evidence on that never came up in this Chamber. We lost on that issue. In effect, the way we view the initial judgement of the Appeals Chamber as it affects Delic was to do two things: one, to have the Trial Chamber reassess punishment in view of the reduction in total criminal conduct, because this Chamber found that he had committed only one murder, not two; and second, to determine whether or not the cumulative convictions constituted harmful error. And that is our view of what this Chamber's order to this second Trial Chamber consisted of. I think I've pointed out the differences in views that we have with the other appellants, and if there's any questions from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you say that the issue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You say that the issue never came up in the first Appeals Chamber because you lost on that issue, but you didn't know that you had lost on that issue until some months later when the judgement was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The question really is: You didn't propose any evidence to be considered upon the basis that if you succeeded on your argument that the decision was manifestly excessive, then you would be entitled to bring up-to-date evidence to be considered on a complete resentencing, and you didn't do it. Now, that's either yes or no again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes; in fact, we did not present evidence. I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, the other question I want to ask you: In your reply, you have a reference to a decision of the US Supreme Court, or at least to a reference to a statement made by Justice Scalia, in which he describes something as a proverbial bombshell or blockbuster. Did you cite that case merely because he has used that phrase in relation to something else, or did he deal with this issue that we're concerned with here as to the basis of review of the factual sufficiency of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was because of the language that Justice Scalia used and because it shows that a court can take a second look if there is a blockbuster or a bombshell, not because it's a directly white-horse case to the facts in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you seem to concede that this bombshell or blockbuster that you are trying to make the Kupreskic judgement into is nothing new on this side of the Atlantic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's awfully new on my side of the Atlantic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, yes. The new world may have different ideas. But nevertheless, it's certainly not new law on this side of the Atlantic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Or, I hasten to add, in the northern hemisphere. But you have never referred back to what the Prosecution has put to you about a previous decision of this Tribunal, which raised exactly the same issue upon the same issue as to sufficiency of evidence, and that was in the Kunarac case, on the motion to acquit, and that was given in July 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well before Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And well before the Celebici appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There was no -- you never asked the Appeals Chamber to look at it upon that basis. You used the word "reliability" on a number of occasions, although I think rather interchangeably with "credibility," but you never asked us to look at that upon that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the reason we did not is it's my opinion that a judgement, an opinion from this Chamber on a final judgement, final consideration, is considerably more persuasive and binding than a Trial Chamber's order on a motion for judgement of acquittal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be more binding, but your argument was that this was new to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and it certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It was new to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, Your Honour, to the extent that it was the first time this analysis was used by this Chamber, and binding upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I won't keep asking you the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you have no other explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I assume that you didn't know about Kunarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have overlooked it, and if I did, it's my fault, not my client's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Justice Gunawardana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, If I understood right, you used the word that the first Appeals Chamber vacated the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: So at the time the case went back to the first -- the second Trial Chamber, there was no sentence in respect of these charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my view, in the form -- or substance-over-form view of the Appeals Chamber's initial judgement in Celebici, while it used the words many times "adjustment," under the Statute, what it did was reverse the Trial Chamber's judgement as to sentence, because it did not affirm it and it did not revise it. So the only possibility left is it reversed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: The legal effect would have been completely different if the sentence was vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps "vacated" is the wrong word. "Reversed" would be the word under the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you just tell me where we reversed it? If you look at the disposition, where does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, it's -- looking at the substance of what you did, as opposed to the form, fitting it into the Court's jurisdiction under Article 25, what you did not do was affirm, and you did not revise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And we did not reverse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm asking you where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What you -- "remanded for adjustment," is the phrase that you used, and there's no question about that, Your Honour. I completely agree with you. That is the phrase that you used. The question that I -- rather than taking the position that some of the other appellants take, that you did not have the authority to do that, what I'm saying is you look at the substance of what you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: If you take up the position that the Court has vacated the -- the first Appeal Chamber vacated the order, then the second Trial Chamber, could not have -- could it have affirmed the sentence? I really think that it could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this Chamber did not have the authority to do what it did under the Statute, then the second Trial Chamber would never have obtained jurisdiction over the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: That's a slightly different situation now. If the first Appeals Chamber vacated the order, the second Appeal -- Trial Chamber confirming the sentence if they thought it fit with the acquittal and the cumulative charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that I exactly understood what you're asking, but let me try to answer it. Your Honour, if you could clarify your question just a little bit. I'm not exactly sure what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: If at the time the case went back to the second Trial Chamber there was no sentence in respect to these charges, the first Appeal -- the second Appeal -- Trial Chamber could not have confirmed the sentence or given the same sentence. It was already decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to each of the three appellants, the order from the first Appeals -- from the Appeals Chamber was somewhat different. What it was as to Mr. Mucic was that the initial sentence was manifestly too low; what it was as to Mr. Delic was that there was less criminality; and what it was as to all three was to consider what effect, if any, the cumulative convictions had on the original Trial Chamber's assessment of punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Moran, I draw your attention to paragraph 42 in the decision, in the sentencing judgement of the reconstituted trial court, and I read: "In the case of the three accused, the totality of their criminal conduct has not been reduced by reason of the quashing of the cumulative convictions." I would ask you to comment on that. How do you respond to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The totality of the conduct, the acts that the defendants were convicted of did not change based upon the quashing of the cumulative convictions. That is correct. Now, as to Mr. Delic, there was an appellate acquittal on one of the two murder counts, and so in his case, there was a reduction in the total amount of criminal conduct for which he was found to be responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But with regard to my question which pertained to cumulative convictions, you do agree with this statement of the Trial Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I very much agree with it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Are you not, Mr. Moran, in effect asking our Court to reduce Article 2 sentences on the ground that Article 3 sentences have been quashed as being impermissibly cumulative?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The issue Mr. Delic has presented on that ground is whether or not the Trial Chamber used the correct analysis to determine that the cumulative sentences did not affect the overall sentences that were imposed by the initial Trial Chamber. That is exactly the issue that this Chamber remanded to the Trial Chamber to determine whether or not there was an effect. And the issue that we have presented is that the Trial Chamber here essentially used two separate harmless error rules, two different rules to determine whether or not error was harmful or harmless, and both of them were in the absence of proof of whether the error was harmful or harmless. One is applied to Mr. Mucic and the comments on his failure to testify, where the Trial Chamber said essentially, "In the absence of evidence we will find some harm," and then the Article 3 cumulative conviction issue where the Trial Chamber essentially said, "We find no evidence that it was harmful. Therefore, we're going to make no adjustment." And so the issue that we're presenting to this Chamber, Mr. Delic is presenting, is whether or not the Trial Chamber used the correct legal standard to reach its conclusion, which is a pure legal issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you said earlier on this morning that -- words to the effect that the remit encompassed two purposes. One was to make adjustments dictated by the quashing of the convictions relating to cumulative offences. I see that in the remit. And the other one was this: that the new Trial Chamber should, I think, undertake a reduction of the sentence in the light of the total criminal conduct of your client. What part of the remit would say so? What part of the remit concerns total criminality aside from adjustments to be made for the quashing of cumulative convictions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking for -- I don't have that judgement in front of me tabbed. If you'd like, I will send something to the -- I'll post a submission, one-page letter pointing to the paragraph. But there is a paragraph in the majority opinion from the Appeals Chamber that talks about and it uses the word "adjustment" based on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Total criminality?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Based on the dismissal of the murder count, count 1 murder conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it does use that word "adjustment".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are not now in a position to point to something in the remit. It's a little over a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If it's not in the remit, if I may help. What you are looking for is paragraph 712 and also 713 in the majority judgement as to whether any adjustment should be made in the sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the reference in each case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe I cited that in my brief, but I don't have the tabbed judgement in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But there's nothing -- you agree there's nothing in the remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There's nothing in the remit; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there something that you would like to advert to in paragraphs 712 and 713 which have been helpfully mentioned by Judge Hunt, something which bears on total criminality?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, paragraph 713, for example, says: "The Appeals Chamber has determined that the conviction for Delic on counts 1 and 2 must be quashed on the basis it is not open to the Trial Chamber to have convicted on these counts. It would be convenient when the matter is remitted for the new Trial Chamber --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Now, could we turn to a point mentioned by Judge Hunt. It concerns the blockbuster reference in your briefs. Did you raise the question of sufficiency of evidence, in particular this distinction between credibility and reliability, before the Appeals Chamber on the last occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- when you were before it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that raises a difficulty for you now raising the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is and has to be that Kupreskic is this Chamber's holding on the analysis that this Tribunal should use. That was not available at the time this Chamber ruled in Celebici. It was not available at the time we filed our briefs in Celebici. Maybe I was remiss in not looking at the orders on interlocutory motions in other Chambers, other Trial Chambers. If I was, that is my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask you this question: Underlying your submissions, it appears to me an assumption that the old Appeals Chamber, on that point, took a decision or an approach which is at variance with the Kupreskic jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is that -- is that your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, when you said "the old Appeals Chamber --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is the Appeals Chamber which decided on the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's -- and I think we've briefed this just in general, but it's our position that there is one Appeals Chamber for the ICTY and that's this Chamber. The individual members may change from time to time, but there is only one Appeals Chamber. Now, that having been said, the Kupreskic decision had not been rendered at that time, and I had not asked the Appeals Chamber at that time to consider it in the view of the Kupreskic analysis because I didn't know that there would be a Kupreskic analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put this to you: Assuming that the point was at all adverted to before the Appeals Chamber, did the Prosecution raise an issue about it? Did the Prosecution take the position that the Kupreskic-type analysis was inapplicable, was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they did not because we did not raise the Kupreskic-type analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, I have before me the transcript of the arguments before the Appeals Chamber, dated 7 June 2000, in which Mr. Karabdic was arguing, and at page 497, he said: "I have to stress that identification by voice is highly unreliable and insufficient to show beyond reasonable doubt that this actually happened." Then at page 526, 527, 528, you will see that the Prosecution, in effect, did not contest that proposition about the need, if I may translate that, to be cautious, in assessing evidence based on voice identification. Then in the decision, at page 485, the decision of the Appeals Chamber of 28th of February 2001, there is this which is said: "As is clear from the above discussions, the other matters raised by Delic as undermining the credibility of the witnesses are not, in the view of the Appeals Chamber, of such a character as would require a reasonable Trial Chamber to reject their evidence. The Appeals Chamber is satisfied that on the evidence before the Trial Chamber, it was open to accept what was described as the fundamental features of the testimony." Was it the case that the Prosecution really relied on alternative material for the submission for which it was contending?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in all candor, I do not believe and I do not recall that the issue was joined between the Defence and the Prosecution on that issue as clearly as it should have been. And perhaps Mr. Karabdic and I did not advocate it as well as we should have, and perhaps the Prosecution did not respond to it as clearly as it might have if we'd have had -- if all of us would have had Kupreskic in front of us and had joined the issue in those terms. They were just not joined in those terms, in the terms of Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is it -- finally, is it open to this Bench to take the view that the previous Bench of the Appeals Chamber presumably acted in conformity with the jurisprudence to which you are adverting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in a case that the Prosecution has just distributed to the Court, a Canadian Supreme Court case called Sarson, S-a-r-s-o-n - and it's just presented to you. I got my copy this morning. I saw a copy last night - the -- there is a discussion about changes in the law while a case is "in the judicial system." And what the Court said there, and I think it's to a great extent our position, that when there is a change -- in the case of Sarson, it was a finding that a Canadian Statute was in violation of their Charter of Rights and, therefore, could not be applied, that as long as the case is in the judicial system, then an Appeals Court that is properly seized with the case can correct that error. That is wholly consistent with a holding of the Supreme Court of the United States in a case, and I'll spell this and read the citation slowly so that everybody can get it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And you would say that that applies whether or not the issue, as distinguished from the authority, was referred to in the Court below?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that it makes -- of course, we're not referring it in the court below. We're referring to the analysis in this Chamber. But it is my view that the Kupreskic Turnbull analysis is substantially different than the analysis that had been conducted in earlier cases. And is that a change in the law? It's at least a change in the application of the law, and it's at least a change in the way that the Appeals Chamber analyses factual decisions from the Trial Chambers. And it's a substantial change, and it's the kind of thing that in -- under Sarson and other cases, in the interests of justice can be corrected at least so long as the case is in the judicial system. And Celebici clearly is in the judicial system. It's clearly within your discretion to correct -- to at least relook. And if I'm wrong on my application of the Kupreskic analysis, that's fine. Well, it's not fine, but if I'm wrong on my analysis, I'm wrong, but it's well within this Chamber's discretion to correct that error because the case is still within the judicial system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a question which should go to one of your colleagues, but you are into this issue now. Whereabouts in Celebici, in the first Appeals Chamber's judgement, does it deny that reliability is relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It does not. And indeed in many cases it refers to the question of reliability in relation to the particular matters that you have raised or that you raised there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Despite the fact that your use of "reliability" may well have been interchangeable for "credibility" in your submissions, the Appeals Chamber did in fact consider reliability. Now, you are going a long way, if I may suggest, to say that because you didn't know of something in the Tribunal's jurisprudence that this is new law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is, of course, an evolving jurisprudence and it's a rapidly evolving jurisprudence. But I would suggest that the most important -- you're right. It was new to me. But is it new -- is an order from a Trial Chamber, which is not even a judgement, on a motion for instruction -- for judgement of acquittal, is that law of the Tribunal at the same level that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is decided by this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suggest to you that anybody who knew of it and who didn't try and run it would be derelict in his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I wouldn't disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It wouldn't have mattered if it had been a decision of the Registrar. It is part of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. So it had already been adopted, if you need to adopt such things. After all, this is a court of general jurisdiction in relation to criminal matters. You don't have to find something in writing in everything that we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I am -- if I was remiss in not finding that judgement -- that order, again I will accept full responsibility on that rather than my client having that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I am still not getting an answer to my question. My question was that if counsel had known of it and had not raised it, he would have been derelict in his duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are I think, now confessing that you didn't know of it. Well, that's fair enough. But nevertheless, your whole proposition depends upon this being some sort of new law of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- one, I am confessing I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: After all, this Court, when it decides questions of whether there should be a reversal of a decision, is not always looking in its own written jurisprudence for some proposition. We have to formulate propositions which are known to the law generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that is the way in which it has worked since the beginning. And this was, I think, the third appeal heard by the Appeals Chamber, and there had been several heard from the Rwanda Tribunal, and you will find bits and pieces here and there. But you don't have to find it somewhere in a written judgement of this Chamber in order to raise it before a new Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I would agree with you, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you do agree -- if I may just put this to you: If you do agree, then how can you describe this as new law which somehow brings into account this new world idea of the law of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, it is at least to this extent new law: It is new law in that it is newly binding upon this Chamber. Prior to that, it was not. If it -- is it new law that it came out of the whole cloth? No, it is not. It is not new law out of the whole cloth. Clearly it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, what Judge Hunt is saying there, if I may state it, conforms to a general view that every practising lawyer knows of a distinction between credibility and reliability. A distinction has to be drawn between a principle and cases which illustrate the principle. The case you had in mind illustrated the principle, but the principle pre-existed that case and that is the position which I believe the Appeals Chamber took, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber in the initial appeal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The passage which I read out to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- it was brief, but it didn't have to be longer than that on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The way that I recall framing the issues to the Trial Chamber on initial submission was framed not in the way that you are discussing reliability as opposed to credibility. I may very well be wrong. I may have said something somewhere in a brief. Lord knows I wrote enough on that case. Too much. But as I recall the way the issues were presented in general to this Chamber was she couldn't remember anything or you couldn't -- it was mainly a credibility. And even if you believe this witness, that, standing alone, was insufficient to justify and to sustain a conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moran. There being no other questions, you may take your seat. Then we will hear Mr. Kuzmanovic, who will speak to us on, I think, the right to silence. Ready, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Morrison and I will share our -- the time that I have, and I will begin by discussing what the Court correctly termed the right of silence. I may have mentioned it as the Fifth Amendment issue because that's the issue that I'm most familiar about but it's actually a 21(4)(g) issue, which is contained in the Article. Before I talk about that 21(4)(g) issue, I would like to talk very briefly about the sentencing standard. We've talked at some length about that. Mr. Murphy and Mr. Moran have both talked about that. But in our view, Your Honours, we believe that the new Trial Chamber failed to follow the standard analysis in taking in account not only the gravity of the offence in sentencing but the individual circumstances. And we believe that the new Trial Chamber did not follow paragraph 787 of the Appeals Chamber's decision. And I quote that section of the paragraph: "It is essential that the sentencing Judge is in possession of the fullest information possible concerning the defendant's life and circumstances." And in our view, the new Trial Chamber, in not getting specific information about our particular client and updating that information did not have the fullest information possible concerning his life and circumstances. We did not see any indication pointing to the record that the new Trial Chamber exercised any analysis of this second factor, and we believe that's an essential part of the sentencing standard that has evolved at the Tribunal. Other than presumably what it had reviewed in the written judgements, the only real observation of our particular client was in the few times that we had either as a Status Conference or during the course of argument. So we believe that it's difficult, if not impossible, for a sentencing Judge or Judges to have the fullest extent of information possible when it merely has the record only before it on a resentence. With respect to the 21(4)(g) issue, the right of silent, we are adamant that this particular issue is fundamental. And we note that the Appeals Chamber, in paragraph 783 of its decision, said that this was an absolute prohibition including sentencing. The prohibition of a negative inference of the failure to testify. I have provided both the Prosecution and the Appeals Chamber with two cases, and believe me, it took a great deal of time and effort of digging around to find something with at least some similar fact pattern and situation in which this principle can be demonstrated. Obviously this is from an American standpoint, and I did look at more than just the American case law on this, but the two cases that I've submitted, one defines the principle, and the other is an Appellate Court's decision on that principle, applying it to the particular facts of that same case. And the two case, Your Honours, I'm referring to, the United States Supreme Court case is Mitchell versus the United States, which was a 1999 case. And the subsequent Appeals Court decision was again United States versus Mitchell, applying what the Supreme Court said in that case to the particular facts. I won't get bogged down in detail in the facts, but suffice it to say that I think one of the more important issues discussed in the remand portion of the Appellate Court decision applying the Supreme Court decision was the fact that the government in that particular case -- there was an argument as to whether or not sentence should be vacated, with the government saying that the -- there is no need to do so because existing record would support the Trial Court's initial decision, and with the counsel for the accused arguing that the sentence should be vacated. And the bottom line in that situation was that after the submissions, the Appeals Chamber said, "Look, we don't have the original Judge here. If we had the original Judge here, that would be an easy decision for us to make. But original Judge is not here. He has since retired from the Bench. And the only fair way to do it would be to have a full rehearing in front of a new Judge." And while not necessarily needing or requesting a full hearing on the issue of sentencing, we believe that at minimum the new Trial Chamber should have had before it the full circumstances and full updating, so to speak, of Mr. Mucic's life and circumstances at the time that it was going to make its decision. Based on those two cases, Your Honour, those are my particular submissions. I will reserve of the balance of my time for Mr. Morrison unless there are questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, in relation to the Court of Appeals when it was sent back to them in the Mitchell case, you will notice that they did consider whether they should send a limited issue to a court but decided in the circumstances of that case it would not be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But they contemplated that it could have been appropriate to have sent a limited issue back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- that's correct, Your Honour. And I any in that particular instance the limited issue could have been sent back had, in my view, in my reading, the original Trial Judge been available. And I think had we had the original Trial Chamber available, I don't think we would have that issue to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, can we assume that your objection to the process that was adopted is that it was wrong because the original Trial Chamber, or at least some Judges of it, were not available but it would have been within the jurisdiction of the Appeals Chamber to have sent a limited issue back to be determined?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think at least as it pertains to my client, a limited issue could have been sent back as long as the Trial Judge or the Trial Chamber in that point on that full life characteristics available and a full updating, for example, of Mr. Mucic's life and characteristics at the time that it had to make that decision. And that wasn't done in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. We will hear your colleague now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to raise just one matter. It's in line with what His Honour Judge Hunt referred to a few moments ago this morning, that the Court is a Court of general determination in criminal law. And what I want to invite Your Honours to develop is a sense of disquiet about one aspect of Mr. Mucic's case. It is plain and it was recognised by the Appeals Chamber that the criticism by the original Trial Chamber concerning Mr. Mucic's failure to testify was unsustainable. In purporting to give full effect to that criticism, the resentencing Trial Chamber elected to reduce the sentence that they thought was appropriate from ten years down to nine years, thus a reduction of one year. In my submission, the object of the exercise was to give full effect to the Appeals Chamber's determination that the original Trial Chamber was in error. And to give full effect to that criticism, one had to reduce the sentence by a measure of the damage that the original determination might have given. And I say "might have given" because I refer back to the -- what's in the judgement of the second resentencing Chamber at paragraph 21. The last two sentences, or three sentences: "The Appeals Chamber held that the Trial Chamber erred in making the remark." The remark that was in error was he, Mr. Mucic, had declined to give any oral evidence, notwithstanding the dominant position he played in the facts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please read slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It goes on: "Since in the context it is indicated that the Trial Chamber regarded the failure in adverse light, and whilst not clear that the Trial Chamber treated Mucic's failure to testify as an aggravating circumstance, the remark left open the real possibility that it did so."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are being asked to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I am sorry. "The Trial Chamber is directed to," and I quote,"consider the effect, if any, of that error on the sentence to be imposed on Mr. Mucic." The consideration of the effect that was directed by the Appeals Chamber to the resentencing Tribunal was heard and is set out in paragraph 27, and it was dealt with in this way, paragraph 27 of the redetermination judgement: "As to the original Trial Chamber's adverse comment as to Mucic's failure to testify during his trial, it is not possible for this Trial Chamber to ascertain the precise effect, if any, which the comment may have upon his sentencing." Well, I stop there. That, with respect, must be right. It was not possible for any Trial Chamber to ascertain the precise effect of the previous Trial Chamber. The previous Trial Chamber was no longer in existence and the Judges were no longer Judges of this Tribunal. They go on to say: "However, the Trial Chamber is not in a position to say that it had no effect. Under those circumstances, the Trial Chamber is of the view that since it may have had an effect, the original sentence should be reduced accordingly." But they then go on to underline how they view that, and they say this: "However, this can be given proper effect by a small reduction." They recognise in paragraph 27 that the one year reduction is a small reduction. The disquiet I invited Your Honour to entertain is this: that the defective reasoning - and that that is the only way to properly describe it in the original Trial Chamber's determination as to Mr. Mucic's failure to testify - was so manifest in a system where the burden of standard of proof remains upon the Prosecution, and it's so basic a defect that it goes to the heart of the whole criminal process. Where a defect goes to the heart of the criminal process, or where it might have gone to the heart of the criminal process, then the redress has to be as fundamental as the original error may well have been. My submission is simple. One year is not a fundamental redress. Even if the sentence - and I say that for the limited purpose of this aspect of the appeal - even if the sentence of ten years was held to be appropriate, the reduction of one year, in my respectful submission, was little more than a gesture towards redressing the balance. The reduction for a fundamental error ought to be fundamental in equity and law; it ought to be a great deal more than 10 per cent. That is a matter for discretion. It's not a matter for my discretion; it's a matter for Your Honours' discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, you say that this was so manifest, this error. One would have expected, would we not, for the Trial Chamber to have given other than a manifestly inadequate sentence for your client? If they had given an enormous sentence, you would draw the inference fairly easily that they had given a considerable amount of weight to this issue. One of the things that was being sent back to the Trial Chamber, as the judgement makes clear, is to find out what effect it had. So they had to start off with the fact that a seven-year sentence had been imposed, which had been held to be manifestly inadequate. That does not suggest, or at least it does not suggest to me, that the Trial Chamber had given such a fundamental effect to this mistake they made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: With great respect, Your Honour, the fact that the original Trial Chamber may have been grossly in error as to more than one aspect of its reasoning is even more reason to entertain disquiet rather than less, because we cannot know, and it may be that in determining the sentence of seven years, they had taken into account the defect, as they perceived it, in him not giving evidence, by increasing an original grossly defective sentence of, say, three and a half years. They might have doubled it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You ask us, then, to assume that they were not only wrong in the assessment of seven years, but they were grossly wrong, because they probably started at three and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, yes, but a possibility isn't sufficient, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: A possibility -- where there has been a series -- I temper what I say, of course, out of respect to the former members of the original Trial Chamber. Where there have been a series of manifest errors in a judgement, the best policy, in my respectful submission, for an appellate tribunal is to take a very long and distant view of the original decisions and reapply the basic principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you do have to show that the Trial Chamber erred in some identifiable way. Was it outside the exercise of their discretion to say that because it was impossible - and after all, they saw the history of it - that one year was sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Two points. First of all, of course, this is an appeal not from the original Trial Chamber, and therefore the determination of the original Trial Chamber is, as it were, passed into history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was talking about the second Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Was there an error that they made in assessing one year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, because if the defect is a defect that goes to the heart of the system, and effectively a reversal or an ignoring of the burden and standard of proof, which is what it amounts to, it's such a fundamental defect that the redress has to be seen by an impartial observer, somebody in the public gallery looking inside and saying, "That was a defective piece of reasoning, a fundamentally defective piece of reasoning. It went to the heart of the burden and standard of proof in a criminal case." What is the redress going to be? Is the redress going to be nominal or is the redress going to be fundamental? If they walk out of the building saying the redress has been nominal, they may not have a great deal of confidence in the system. If they walk out of the building saying,"It's not exactly what I would have done, but, yes, that's a fundamental redress," then there is confidence in the system, and that is the general consideration of criminal jurisdiction, about which I have no doubt Your Honour was referring a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that what you're trying to do is to obtain compensation for your client for the error the Trial Chamber made, if I may put it as baldly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't think the word passed my lips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, but that's the effect of it. You're saying that the Trial Chamber should have disregarded what they thought would be an appropriate sentence, without the reference to the impermissible observation, by overcompensating your client so that the public would understand how fundamental the error had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: First and foremost, in my submission, the error is inarguably fundamental. It's about as basic an error as one would expect to see coming out of a court dealing with an adversarial system where the burden and standard of proof lies upon the Prosecution. I'm sorry if those are in strong terms, but it is; it's a basic and fundamental error. It's the sort of error that if one made it as an advocate standing in court in my jurisdiction, you'd have your ears pulled off by the judge. It's that fundamental. And therefore, to maintain a degree of confidence in the system, where there has been a fundamental error, even if it was a question of overcompensating - and I don't concur, with great respect, that it is. I say it's simply a proper balancing exercise - it is better that it is seen to be -- that that sort of error is seen to be so dismissed that it will not occur again in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suppose it would be a fairly fundamental error by a Trial Chamber to overlook the fact that the accused had spent two years in custody before the trial and hadn't taken that into account in the sentence to be imposed. That would be fairly fundamental, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Depending on the circumstances of the case, it may well be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But you wouldn't suggest, would you, that the sentence should be adjusted by more than the period that the fellow had spent in custody awaiting the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It may, in the circumstances, if the period in custody was so fundamental, it may amount to an abuse of process, and there may be an argument as to that, but that would be an argument which would have been raised before trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you found any authority for this sort of approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Equity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's not an authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It's a principle, and it's a principle upon which this Court is founded, all courts are founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Equity means a fair adjustment. You're asking for an overcompensatory one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a matter for discretion. If you ask me that question and expect me to agree with it, I would respectfully decline to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Gunawardana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances in which the trial had made the observation in respect of what circumstances relating to the accused that he said an adverse inference can be drawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, is Your Honour asking me what the original Trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: -- Trial Chamber said? That is to be found -- I'm sorry. It is alluded to in the judgement of the second sentencing Tribunal. It's at paragraph 21, Your Honour. I quote. The whole paragraph bears reading: "The final matter relating to Mr. Mucic concerns remarks made by the Trial Chamber, when imposing sentence upon him, when it said that the accused had made concerted and sustained efforts where he could intimate," that must be intimidate, "witnesses and to suborn favourable evidence from them." That was a subject of a -- there was no evidence as to that, and that was a subject of a separate complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
