utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. My client has been signalling me. He would like to have -- could he have a five-minute recess or a ten-minute recess?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, would it be convenient, then, if we suspended at this time for 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Your Honour's question. The answer must be yes, because, as it were, my convenience is matched by the defendant's inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We'll suspend for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber stands resumed. Mr. Morrison, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Much obliged. Your Honour, I had just reached the part of paragraph 21 where the original Trial Chamber indicated in their judgement about Mr. Mucic, and I quote: "His demeanour throughout the proceedings suggests that he appears to have regarded this trial as a farce and an expensive joke." All I can say about that is that that was purely, obviously, the Trial Chamber's view of Mr. Mucic. There's no evidence one way or the other as to how he regarded the trial. That is simply, in my respectful submission, a prejudicial remark which is uneasy, in light of what they immediately say afterwards: "He has declined to give any oral evidence, notwithstanding the dominant position he played in facts giving rise to the prosecution of the accused persons." They there make the juxtaposition between his declination to give evidence and their view that he held a dominant position. In those circumstances, in my respectful submission, they must have held that as a very prejudicial feature of the case, otherwise why make the remarks as they did, in those terms and in the context of what they said before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: May I just go back, Your Honours, to deal with the matter, having had the opportunity to think about it a little more. His Honour Judge Hunt made the observation about the comparison between somebody being in custody pre-trial. Thinking about that, with great respect, there can be no real nexus between somebody being in custody pre-trial, because that doesn't affect any prejudicial view of the Tribunal during the course of the trial itself. It's a separate issue. But what it might come to is this. And one always hesitates to draw upon personal experience, but I must, because it illustrates the matter nicely. I have been involved in a case where a person in England was waiting, not in custody, but simply waiting for trial for three years, for no other reason than the Crown Prosecution service had been dilatory. When it came to his trial, he was duly tried for stealing money from the company in which he worked and was convicted and sentenced. Inevitably, he was sentenced to a custodial sentence for breach of trust. The trial judge made the remark - in my submission, quite properly - that he was reducing the sentence passed upon the defendant because of the amount of time he had spent in custody -- amount of time he had spent waiting for his trial, and therefore the inevitable stress and strain upon him was greater than it would have been for most people. So in as far as there's an analogy at all, it would be a proper analogy, in my respectful submission, at the sentencing stage but not at the determination of guilt or innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. One small question, Mr. Morrison. You were good enough to give us your experience in your jurisdiction, and you said something to the effect that the right to silence was absolute and a member of the bar who infringed that right would be in danger of having his ears pulled. What has happened with the 1994 United Kingdom act which I believe qualified the right of silence in certain ways? Has it been repealed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No, no. With great respect, Your Honour misunderstood the analogy I was making. I wasn't saying that the right of silence was as sacrosanct in my jurisdiction. I only wish it was. I said that in many jurisdictions it's sacrosanct, where there's an adversarial process. What I meant to say was, or what I meant to say was - and I think the transcript will bear me out - that if an advocate made an error as basic as that, not necessarily that error, but an error as basic as that, in front of a Tribunal, he would be heavily criticised for it. It's the seriousness of the error, not necessarily the actual context of the error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you weren't necessarily adverting to the position in your own jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I wish I could. It's a source of, for me personally, some embarrassment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you have a case which went to the European Court of Human Rights, and that court, in effect, held - I believe I'm correct in this, but I'm open to qualification - that the right to silence may be varied depending on the strength of the case which the accused has to meet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Under the HCR ruling in the case in point, and I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Murray's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. -- is that Strasbourg determined it to be a qualified right and one of proportionality, and proportionality is one of the features of the Human Rights Act in the United Kingdom that gives effect to the HCR legislation. But we are blessed in this Tribunal that we don't have the 1994 act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good. But we have this, do we: We have it from the Appeals Chamber, after a thorough and careful examination of comparative jurisdictions, that the right is absolute and it applies to the sentence stage as well. But now there's a question of waiting, waiting the effect of a breach of that right, say as it pertains to the conviction stage and as it pertains to the sentencing stage. Could we properly, in your opinion, take into account the qualifications which exist in certain jurisdictions on the operation of that right to weight the effect of the breach of the right? In this case, after all, the adverse comment made by the Trial Chamber occurred during the sentencing stage, I believe, and not during the conviction stage. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It would be disingenuous to suppose that an appellate chamber couldn't take that view, but it would have to be, in my respectful submission, very sure that it could determine with some certainty the degree of prejudice that had actually had been engendered, and the difficulty is in most cases - and it's certainly the difficulty in this case - that one cannot tell. It is speculative as to the degree of prejudice that was applied by the original Trial Chamber. It's not as speculative as it might be, because we can see the comments in paragraph 21, where they're not only saying he declined to give oral evidence, but the accused was criticised for his demeanour, and indeed quite falsely - and I say that without reproach, because there was no evidence of it - made concerted and sustained efforts to intimidate witnesses. There was no basis for that remark whatsoever. There was no evidence. And had there been a suggestion he had done that, he would have faced contempt proceedings. That was, with respect, a curiously prejudicial remark. But to go back to Your Honour's question: Plainly, if it was possible, by an analysis of the judgement, if the judgement had been so carefully written and had descended into such particulars that you could see exactly what the extent and formation of the prejudice was, then the approach of the Appeal Chamber could well be one that Your Honour advocates. It would have been an extremely dangerous approach, in my submission, and likely to be -- the temptation might be in those circumstances to - subconsciously at least - to submerge the principle under the facts, and in my respectful submission, the principle must always prevail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. You have been very helpful. On behalf of the Bench, I thank all counsel who have spoken on behalf of the appellants. I would now turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. There are some individual issues left to be dealt with by Mr. Moran and then by Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. I think that in the questioning we pretty well got into all of the issues we've raised. Mr. Karabdic is going to discuss in a little bit of detail the Kupreskic analysis and how it applies to the cases that we have. I think the only other thing that I would just stress is on the issues of presenting mitigating evidence. We clearly, I think, preserve that error in the Trial Chamber. We presented what we thought we could prove, and the Trial Chamber wouldn't even accept that filing. With that, Your Honour, Mr. Karabdic will discuss the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karabdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours and the Presiding Judge of this Chamber mentioned that at the previous hearing before the Appeals Chamber, I spoke about the unacceptability of identification, voice identification, and my submissions were not accepted, because at that time this Tribunal had different law. In the Kupreskic case a completely different position was taken when much stricter criteria were applied for identification. In that case, the position of the English and American law was accepted, and this position was presented in the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Kupreskic case, thus becoming the law of this Tribunal. So this is a new case law for this Tribunal. Therefore, Mr. Delic has a right to request that the new, more advantageous law be applied to him, the new law that has been adopted in the meantime. And in light of this new case law, the testimony that was admitted in the original trial would not be accepted now, notwithstanding the fact that the Trial Chamber was of the view that those witnesses spoke what they believed to be the truth. However, this truce [as interpreted] of theirs and their testimony in general was not acceptable enough to come to the conclusion that Delic in fact did call out the name of the late Milosevic. In addition to that, I would also like to state that there are two witnesses, Novica Djordjic and Milenko Kuljanin who said that they recognised the voice. However, these two witnesses were contradictory in their presentation and description of this entire event. We have mentioned this on earlier occasions. This Tribunal is well aware of the fact that the Prosecution has a statement of one of the witnesses in which it is said that that inmate in the tunnel number night [as interpreted] on that fateful night recognised the voice of a completely different person, not of Mr. Delic. In view of that, I believe that the -- that the request for revision should be granted and that Mr. Delic should be acquitted on this count. This is dictated not only by the interest of justice but also by the duty of this Tribunal to base it's decisions on the truth alone. I think that what was determined in the original judgement is seriously undermined now and that this conclusion is not in accordance with the new law adopted in the Kupreskic case. I would like to say that for us continental lawyers, this may seem somewhat unusual. However, in the common law system which is applied here, there is case law which becomes law by the judgements being passed and that case law has the same value as the statutory law. Do any of Your Honours have any questions regarding this? I would also like to say something about the sentence. My learned colleague made his submissions claiming that the Trial Chamber did not act in accordance with the decision of the Appeals Chamber, the second Trial Chamber. However, I would like to say that within the instructions given to the second Trial Chamber, this Trial Chamber did not adhere to them. This Trial Chamber put into the instructions received from the Appeals Chamber the words "if any," and it did so completely on its own, thus hurting the interests of my client. In doing so, the Trial Chamber disobeyed the fact that the instructions of the Appeals Chamber are mandatory for the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber also through -- the Trial Chamber violated the right of my client to have his sentence reduced in accordance with paragraph 1 of the Appeals judgement. Many arguments and many things that -- that are in favour of my client were thus disregarded. And it should not have been so because that was contrary to the instructions of the Appeals Chamber. The second error made with respect to the sentencing, made by the Trial Chamber, is -- is the one that pertains to the length of discussion of the deeds that were still attributed to Mr. Delic. And based on the analysis of the graveness of these deeds, the Trial Chamber issued a new sentence, which in my opinion is a trial de novo, at least with respect to the sentence. The Trial Chamber assessed the mitigating circumstances on its own without giving an opportunity to the parties to present their arguments on the issue. The Trial Chamber also completely neglected the mitigating circumstances, both those that were presented by the counsel of the accused and those that were acknowledged in the initial judgement of the initial Trial Chamber. In my opinion, the 20-year sentence should be taken as such -- should have been taken as such by the Trial Chamber and analysed the extent to which the conviction on count 1 affected the length of the sentence. This crime under count 1 was the gravest crime for which Mr. Delic was prosecuted, and it pertained to the murder of an old, feeble, ill man, a murder committed out of base motives, a murder that was committed as a revenge. It is true that this crime is what mostly led to the sentence of my client. Therefore, the Chamber should have assessed that fact and adjust the sentence accordingly. A sentence so adjusted would be a sentence for total criminal behaviour of Mr. Delic less the crime under count 1. However, under Article 41 of the Criminal Code of Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which under Article 65 of this Tribunal's Statute is applied or should be taken into account when sentencing the accused, sets forth that in sentencing, the Chamber should also analyse the social danger of the deed as well as the social danger posed by the perpetrator. This reduction of the sentence to which I alluded so far would only pertain to the reduction of sentence which is caused by the reduced social danger of the crime committed. However, after vacating the conviction under count 1, Delic may not be considered a person -- the same person that was described in the Trial Chamber judgement. All of these negative characteristics given by the Trial Chamber in its judgement are mostly based on his conviction under count 1. Therefore, I think that since it is established that Mr. Delic is not the kind of person he was believed to be by the Trial Chamber, the original Trial Chamber, a further reduction is due because he is not the dangerous person he was described by the original Trial Chamber. Therefore, I believe that the proposal we gave in our appeals brief is well grounded. Any questions, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. We will now give the floor to Ms. Sinatra who will speak to us on individual issues which remain in respect of Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. We were given an instruction not to regurgitate our briefs, and so I intend to make this as brief as possible. I just wanted to bring to the attention of the Court that during the Kupreskic discussion earlier, Judge Hunt astutely and correctly brought to our attention that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is based upon general principles of justice and general principles of fundamental law whether we find it written in one of these case studies or not. And Mr. Landzo and the other appellants in this case, we all agree with that premise. We are here out of the principles of fairness. We also support and agree with the arguments proposed by Mr. Mucic regarding the fundamental unfairness of the interpretation by the second Trial Chamber of the first Trial Chamber -- of the first Appeals Chamber's mandate. And the first Appeals Chamber stated that it remits to a Trial Chamber to be nominated by the President of the Tribunal the issue of what adjustment, if any, should be made to the original sentences imposed on Hazim Delic, Zdravko Mucic and Esad Landzo to take account of the dismissal of these counts. The Trial Chamber further ordered that the calling of further evidence was unnecessary since the Appeals Chamber had defined the issues so narrowly. And the Trial Chamber, the second Trial Chamber, rejected any attempt by the appellants to -- by the accused to introduce any further evidence at that time. So if we look at Article 24(2) and Rule 101(B), we can understand that the requirements of those under sentencing, no matter which Trial Chamber it is, would require further evidence. The current circumstances of the accused must be reflected in any new sentence. Instead, what we found were three new strangers on a second Trial Chamber and who at minimum should have heard evidence regarding the current circumstances of the accused prior to sentencing. This is the same kind of fundamental principle of law that Judge Hunt referred to earlier. As far as the cumulative charging and sentencing is concerned, we support and we also find relevance in the propositions and suggestions of Judge Hunt and Judge Bennouna in their separate opinions in the first appeal. I think that that warrants -- I know that you have this before you, but just for the record, the authors of the separate opinion recognised certain issues that apply to sentencing why evidence should have been presented and how this sentencing affects not only how much time the accused will be serving but also where he will serve his sentence, whether he will be allowed to be patrolled. And the authors say secondly - sorry - "We give our reasons as to why cumulative convictions in relation to the same conduct, as well as cumulative penalties in sentencing are impermissible. The fundamental question raised by this issue is that it is necessary to avoid any, any prejudice being caused to an accused by being penalised more than once in relation to the same conduct. Prejudice to the rights of the accused are the very -- or the very real risk of such prejudice lies in allowing cumulative convictions." I'm sure this Court is familiar with this separate opinion, but it goes on and on to explain how the sentence, even if the sentence remained the same after they dismissed the Article 3 convictions, that this sentence will affect future decisions on sentencing, release, parole, and rights of the accused while being detained. Well, at this point, I think we agree with the arguments of Mucic and my esteemed colleague Mr. Murphy and we would like to reserve the right for rebuttal after the Prosecution's position. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sinatra. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I hope I'm correct this time in saying that that ends the case for the appellants. If so, I do give the floor to leading counsel for the Prosecutor, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be speaking in relation to two matters - excuse me, Your Honour. I'll be speaking in relation to two matters this morning and then my colleagues will speak to what are essentially the substantive issues in the Prosecution's submission on the appeal. The three real or substantive issues relate to the effect of the dismissal of the cumulative conviction, the effect of the adverse comment to testify and the effect in Mr. Delic's case of the quashing of convictions. The dismissal -- the effect of the dismissal of the cumulative convictions and the affect of the adverse comment to testify will be dealt with by my colleague Ms. Brady, and the effect of quashing the convictions will be dealt with by my colleague Mr. Carmona. There are two other issues, somewhat preliminary matters, that are raised by the appellants or at least one of the appellants, and the other appellants. One relates to jurisdiction, and the other relates to a request by Mr. Delic to reconsider the original Appeals Chamber's decision in light of Kupreskic. It's those two, as I would submit, preliminary matters, the jurisdictional issue and the review based on Kupreskic, which I will address. I hope, in light of the time, to finish simply within about 15 or 20 minutes and leave some time for questions and then allow my colleagues to speak, so I'll simply start with the first issue, which is the jurisdictional one. Essentially, the submission of the appellants is that they wanted a complete rehearing on sentence. They have, therefore, formulated their ground of appeal to try and achieve that result. They attack the remittal on the basis that there was no jurisdiction to remit, and then they proceed to do an interpretation both under Article 25 and Rule 117. First, before dealing with that issue, the first submission I wish to make, quite simply, is that these appellants are asking this Appeals Chamber to review its decision that it implicitly had the power to remit. I appreciate the distinction of Mr. Murphy that the appeal was from the Trial Chamber's refusal on their motion to jurisdiction, but as you recall, the motion itself was that the Appeals Chamber did not have the authority to remit. So -- and therefore, it was actually challenging a decision of the Appeals Chamber and is now seeking to challenge that again. As it is essentially a motion for reconsideration, they put forward two submissions essentially. One, that the decision was per in curiam and that the other was there were no submissions made on this issue. With respect, it's the Prosecution's position that the Appeals Chamber clearly addressed their mind to this issue, was fully informed of it. The Appeals Chamber was fully aware, of course, of its previous decision in Tadic where it recognised the right to remit, and obviously was aware of the issue in Tadic where it was remitted for a particular purpose. The second submission they've made is that there was no submissions on this issue before the Appeals Chamber, and, therefore, they should be permitted to raise the issue, the jurisdictional issue, now that's in their briefs. There were no submissions made on this issue, that's correct. But as we know from the Appeals Chamber's decision in Jelisic, the right to make submissions is generally in situations where a party's rights are affected. The rights that they claim which are affected are the right to introduce mitigating evidence and their right to make submission on the change in the law since their original sentence. With respect, there is no right to admit mitigating evidence on the resentence. In fact, if the Appeals Chamber can revise, as they did in Aleksovski, without hearing any mitigating evidence at the point of revision after it was determined that the sentence was unjust, the Appeals Chamber, therefore, has demonstrated that they don't -- are not required to hear mitigating evidence at the time of the resentence be it by the Appeals Chamber on a revision or be it by the Trial Chamber. As well as, we're aware from the President's decision in Kolundzija where the President released Mr. Kolundzija on early release, the President took into consideration the post-conduct -- I'm sorry, post-trial or post-conviction conduct, and therefore there is a right to hear this material, hear this evidence. Regarding their other right or their claim that they were prejudiced, which is they were not able to make submissions on the subsequent decisions, the subsequent jurisprudence, with respect, the issue of parity is not applicable. The Appeals Chamber determined, based on full submissions and argument, what the appropriate sentence was for these three appellants. The subsequent case law of this Tribunal cannot, therefore, change the original decision of the Appeals Chamber and the issue of parity is something which can be raised when you challenge the sentence itself. It's not something that you can ask for a re-visitation of your sentence. In light of those submissions, it's submitted that the Appeals Chamber's implicit decision to remit cannot be appealed in this case, and the Appeals Chamber did make a determination that it had the authority to remit at that time. And unless the Court grants leave to reconsider its implicit decision, that matter has already been dealt with by the Appeals Chamber. Those would be my submissions on an initial preliminary issue about whether or not this can even be raised at this stage. Regarding the substantive issue of jurisdiction, I simply make one point. The appellants state that where the law -- sorry, the Statute is unambiguous, it cannot be interpreted to result in the approach that the Prosecution submits, and they point to Article 25, I think it's fair to submit that Article 25 is not an Article which is unambiguous on this issue. There's no power to remit specifically, expressly stated under Article 25. It's not an unambiguous interpretation. Article 25 does not give -- under the specific wording does not say the word "remit." In fact, as this Court has already stated, Article 25 doesn't even permit an appeal against sentence. But this Court has found that it's implied. Clearly it's implied in the reversal, that if the matter is reversed or if the matter is dealt with by the Appeals Chamber, it certainly must have the power to remit. And Rule 117(C), according to the appellants' argument is, in my respectful submission, is that 117(C) therefore limits the authority under Article 25. They admit there's a power to remit. They admit that it's implied under Article 25. But then they say the power to remit has to be only for a full sentencing because look at Article 117(C). Well, with respect that's backwards. Article 235 of the Statute is the enabling legislation which creates the power to remit in the first place. Rule 117 doesn't limit the power to remit, it simply is a procedure if you do remit the matter back or if you do -- you do have the authority of the procedure for sending it back for retrial. If I can just, secondly, deal with their reliance on Tadic. The appellants argue that Tadic is not authority -- sorry, is authority for remittal but not authority for remittal for a limited purpose. With respect, that was never addressed in Tadic. It was not a submission that was dealt with in Tadic, and it was not specifically addressed by the Court. But what's interesting is that Tadic, in fact, unless I may have misunderstood Mr. Murphy's submissions, but if I haven't, the Landzo reply brief, I think it's at paragraph 5, seems to state that the Tadic remittal was a new trial on the issue of sentencing as a whole. With respect, it wasn't. What happened in Tadic was that it was not -- it didn't consider all the -- taking into account all the previous offences for the accused for which he'd originally been convicted as is stated in the reply brief, unless I've misread it. It only sent it back on the ones for which the Prosecution appeal was successful. So it didn't accepted it back for a new full hearing on all the offences, it sent it back for a limited purpose which is those sentences for which the Prosecution's appeal should result in conviction. So with respect, it did permit a remittal for a narrower issue than a full sentencing on all the counts. Then the next point is, well, could it then be sent back for even a narrower issue, which is a remittal on the three issues for which there was an error? And with respect, I see no reason either in the law or in the Statute, in the terms of the Statute, which would result in anything different. And lastly, I note once again that though it wasn't specifically addressed, the Appeals Chamber in Kupreskic decided to take into consideration in relation to Mr. Santic a matter with respect to his cooperation. This is post-trial. There was cooperation by Mr. Santic, and it was raised as part of his sentence. The Kupreskic Appeals Chamber, it was submitted by the Prosecution, could do two things. They could sent it back, if they felt it necessary, on that single issue, or they could actually decide it themselves. In my submission, in paragraphs 461 and 462 of Kupreskic, the Appeals Chamber recognised it had the authority to remit it back on that single issue, but the wording it stated was that the Appeals Chamber decided it was not necessary in the facts of this case. Once again, though it's not specifically addressed, it is implicitly recognised. And lastly, addressing the claim that even if there was a limited hearing, they should have -- mitigating evidence should have been heard in any event, that that denial created some type of prejudice or unfairness. Without resubmitting, the hearing was for a limited purpose. The mitigating evidence up and to the point of trial was dealt with by the Trial Chamber and reviewed by the Appeals Chamber. There was no mitigating evidence submitted at the time of the Appeals Chamber, so essentially the time we're looking at is not actually from the first Trial Chamber to the second Trial Chamber but presumably the time frame when they claim they couldn't put it forward, which would be from February 2001 until October 2001, which was the new sentencing date. In my respectful submission, there is no error in not permitting at the second sentencing hearing the mitigating evidence. As I stated in Aleksovski, when they revised the decision, they didn't take into consideration mitigating evidence, and I don't think there's an assertion that that was an error. As well, though it's not directly on point, the Appeals Chamber in Jelisic has held that post-conviction conduct, specifically in Jelisic he attempted to put forward a report from the detention centre was not found to be admissible on the appeal. Now, it's arguable that the reason that -- this is also found and noted by the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber in footnote 741. Now, it's arguable that the Jelisic Appeals Chamber declined to hear post-conviction conduct on the basis that it could not be used to attack the sentence. The sentencing judgement clearly couldn't have been in error because it didn't have that conduct before it. I won't go through it now, but I draw your attention to the language. It's -- it's a little uncertain in that the language in Jelisic was that the post-sentence behaviour is not relevant to any issue before the Trial Chamber - that's understandable - nor is it capable of being considered by it. Now, it doesn't really make sense because, of course, it wouldn't even be available at the time it considered. But if what it's saying is that that type of conduct is not relevant to the initial sentencing, then the analysis is one of what is the purpose for which the Chamber addresses the sentencing issue? In my submission, the initial Trial Chamber has a full hearing and therefore, of course, it's considered. Appeals Chamber will not accept post-conviction conduct because of the nature of its hearing. It's not a new sentencing hearing. It's to review the original sentencing hearing. The Appeals Chamber has the discretion, I would submit, not necessarily to receive mitigating evidence as it did in Aleksovski, and it just revised the sentence once it found there was an error. And where the remittal is for a limited purpose, then once again the Trial Chamber has a discretion in this case to address the issues for which it was remitted, just like in relation to all the other functions performed by either the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber in relation to sentencing and in relation to -- in considering whether they should take into consideration post-conduct behaviour. Those are my submissions on that issue before I move to the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, let's take the situation which I understand to be the usual one in a criminal appeal court where there has been an appeal against sentence. Everybody would agree that it's not a rehearing on sentence and, therefore, additional evidence is not admissible on that issue. But once an error has been accepted, the Appeals Chamber has to revise the sentence, to use the wording of the Statute. It may be that the nature of the error made by the Trial Chamber is such that the Appeals Chamber may consider it is necessary to resentence. Now, in each of the cases here, there was an appeal against sentence, and it was suggested there had to be a resentence. So that if each of the appellants had, as I believe they should have, put on material for consideration only if they had been successful in their appeal against sentence, do you suggest the Appeals Chamber could have refused to hear it? Because that seemed to be the effect of what you were saying earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's the exact issue, Your Honour, and it's an interesting one. In the jurisdictions I'm aware of and I think similar to the ones you're aware of, the Appeals Chamber would probably consider that evidence. The issue is what is it relevant to? It's not relevant to the criminal conduct. It's not mitigating of the criminal conduct. It's not relevant to the original sentence, and it's not relevant to the errors for which the Appeals Chamber has to revise the original sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, certainly the Trial Chamber should have been able to foresee into the future, as well as anybody could, as to what their conduct may be likely to be, for example, on matters of rehabilitation. And if that is a matter which should be taken into account in a resentencing, can the Appeals Chamber refuse to accept it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I think, and I don't want to seem harsh here because I think it's within the discretion of the Appeals Chamber to accept it, the flip side, of course, is what you are implying. Well, then, do they have the discretion to reject it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: And the question is if it is a matter to be considered -- if the sentencing is actually to determine what is the appropriate sentence for the conduct for which the convicted person has been convicted, and if the post-conduct behaviour is relevant, as in Kolundzija, to release, then the Court could. I mean, that's the purpose of the sentence, is something to determine what his sentence should be placing him back at the time in relation to the criminal conduct for which he's been convicted. As long as there's an avenue where that can be considered and it is considered in the release or the execution or service of the sentence, then it may not be an error by the Appeals Chamber to decline to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But aren't you taking a very narrow view of the matters which any sentencing Court have to consider? It's not simply the criminal conduct. It's also prospects of rehabilitation that must be relevant. The -- assume that they had seen the light and were prepared to confess what they had done and that they recognise the error of their ways. The Rules of the Tribunal do not encourage that sort of evidence during the course of the trial because it has to be given in the course of the trial, and there are no longer separate sentencing proceedings, a matter which, to use a phrase I have some unease about. But that is the fact. They can't do it then. Why should they not be entitled to say, "I have seen the error of my ways. I have done a terrible thing, and I have accepted some religious tenets," or something, if they had put it forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Of course and I recognise the distinction you're making and you have made, of course, to my learned colleagues. The first submission is that that is an issue which goes to the execution of the sentence, in my submission. That's an issue that goes to whether or not the person should be released early or what consideration should be given because of the fact that they have in fact admitted guilt or taken steps to find other ways to relieve themselves of the burden. But without trying to mislead the Court, of course I recognise that the Appeals Chamber in Kupreskic has recognised that post-conviction cooperation with the Prosecution is a relevant factor. Therefore, it's, quite frankly, post-conviction conduct. But that -- if I can make one final comment. It may not be assisting any more. But that's because of the specific Rule which indicates that that factor is to be considered, because it appears that the Rules are trying to encourage that sort of conduct. And that's an exception to what I say is the general sentencing regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Gunawardana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: I believe I understood you right. You are saying that the appeal cannot be reheard, in a matter of saying. So that is the position. The reference has always to be limited when you refer it back to the Trial Chamber. The guidance given in this instance was to look at it from the position of the effect on the cumulative charges. So my question is: Can the Appeals Chamber restrict its scope when it makes that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In the Prosecution's submission, yes, it can. There's authority to remit. There's authority to remit for particular purposes. It's been done. And it can remit solely for the purposes that are to be -- where there was some error. In my respectful submission - I mean, I'm just reiterating what is said in the Celebici Appeals Chamber judgement - the purpose for which it's being sent back is not the purpose for which my learned colleagues are asking the sentencing to take place; it was for the limited purpose to correct and to safeguard against any possible errors in result of the three issues that were raised by the Appeals Chamber, and to protect the appeal rights. For that limited purpose, they do have the jurisdiction to send it back, and the Appeals Chamber has recognised the power to remit. The only issue in dispute here, as I've indicated, appears to be the scope of the power to remit, and in my earlier submissions, Your Honour, I have submitted that there is nothing in the Articles or the Rules which prevent it, and the Articles have been interpreted to permit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: In complying with the direction that was given to the Trial Chamber, it is circumscribed to look at the issues and according to only matters related to the issue that is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's my position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One little question, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It's probably not germane to a great deal of the discussion, but I noted with interest your submission that Rule 107(C) therefore limits the authority under Article 25 of the Statute. Do you recall saying words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was putting forward that that would be the ultimate position of the appellants. That's not the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's not the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If one contends for the proposition that a Rule could limit the Statute, what one is contending for is that a Rule could amend the Statute. That is not on, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Clearly, the Prosecution's position is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you also said that the Appeals Chamber, if it were exercising its own competence to resentence, is not required to hear mitigating evidence. Do I recollect right your total submission to be that although the Appeals Chamber is not required to hear mitigating evidence, it may, in a proper case, do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In this case, I believe, somewhere in the text of the judgement there's a reference to a new complete rehearing being required, to be undertaken by the new Trial Chamber, the reconstituted Trial Chamber. Is it possible to entertain an argument where that shows that the Appeals Chamber did make a decision as to whether new evidence was to be heard and that it decided no new evidence is to be heard, and it was on that basis that the remission was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That would be the Prosecution's submission, yes. The specific wording --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Paragraph 712.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: 712 and 713. Thank you. If I may just comment on the second issue, if I can leave this issue. If there's no further questions, I'll speak to the second issue, and in light of the timing, I'll simply just inform you of the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Your time is still running.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Actually, my time, compared to my colleagues, is probably up. The second issue relates to Mr. Delic's request for a review in light of the revolutionary law in Kupreskic. I think the Court clearly, by its questions, is fully aware of the Prosecution's submissions, and I don't think I need to go into them. I'm fully prepared to answer any questions. The Prosecution's position essentially is there's a preliminary issue. Despite the very interesting arguments of whether or not we should adopt the law-of-the-case doctrine or whether res judicata applies, whether this is a final judgement or not final judgement, the issue doesn't even arise if the Court finds that Kupreskic is not a fundamental change in the law. If the Court was to find that it was, then the issue would be whether or not, if there is a change in the law, the Court would be permitted to hear it, whether the conviction is final. And therefore it's res judicata, or whether or not the case remains open. The Prosecution's submission is that when you look at the way the Celebici appeal was argued, the grounds of appeal and the submissions on reliability and credibility, the Appeals Chamber addressed exactly what was requested of it, and it cannot now be faulted for not addressing an issue which was not before it. Secondly, the Appeals Chamber did actually address both credibility and reliability, and therefore this issue doesn't even arise. In light of the fact that I'm cutting into my colleagues' time, unless there are any questions on that issue, which I'd be happy to answer, those are the comments I have to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A small matter. Paragraph 6.16 of your submissions, when you venture into this law-of-the-case doctrine, you say the difference between them is whether there is a final judgement. Now, where does that fit into the law of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not sure if I understand your question. The law of the case is that you can continue to revise up until the point where there's a final judgement. After the final judgement, res judicata kicks in between the parties, and therefore you cannot seek to have a matter revisited if there's an intervening decision. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I thought you were going to say. But when we have a final judgement here, a final judgement on conviction. Is that the final judgement you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's specifically it. And though I wasn't going to get into it, if I may, the final judgement here is the judgement on conviction. And what's interesting is that that has implicitly, despite counsel for Mr. Delic's submissions, in my respectful submission, without taking away his right to comment on this, of course, that's implicitly recognised by Mr. Delic. Mr. Delic filed a motion for review on the basis of new evidence which affected his conviction. He said in his motion for review that he meets all the requirements necessary to bring a review under Rule 119. Now, I don't want to pretend that this issue has been litigated or it's been addressed, but clearly he can't have both. I mean, if it is a final judgement, as determined by Barayagwiza, which ultimately determines the issue, then he can't come now and rely on law-of-the-case doctrine. If it's not a final judgement, then he shouldn't have brought a motion for review, because the matter is still pending before the Appeals Chamber and he could have filed it as additional evidence. But that's not the case. In this case, as well, in the decision on the motion for review, the Appeals Chamber found that there was an ultimate decision, an ultimate or final decision on conviction. Since that is the case, in my respectful submission, you can't reopen up the conviction appeal in the middle of a sentencing hearing, and that's why, despite my friend's comments that the technical arguments were somewhat silly, the Prosecution pointed out that it would have to constitute either one of two -- it would have to constitute a motion for reconsideration properly in relation to a conviction which was final.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You saw the point of the question. The next question is: You, of all people, I think, would be eminently suited to explain to us what the Canadian case means about "in the flow of the litigation," or some such phrase, the case that you've just produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. I actually argued that at the trial level, so I do have some intimate knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's an interesting case, but how does that expression fit into the final decision of the law of the case, which I know comes from a different part of the continent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you. My understanding of the Sarson decision was that if you're still before the court, if you're still in the proceedings, you can raise it. And the argument is that if, during the time from which you are convicted - by the Trial Chamber, of course - and the time that you appeal, the law changes, you're not bound, when you stand before the appellate chamber, to the law that was in effect at the time of the trial chamber. You can rely on subsequent decisions that are in effect and controlling, if I can use the word, at the time of your appeal. If your appeal is final, and two years later there is a change in the law, you cannot come back and try to somehow put yourself back in the system. And in fact, in the Sarson case - it's in the record, so I'm not trying to put any evidence on the record - the applicants in the Sarson case actually first recognised that and went and applied actually for an extension of time to file a notice of appeal. That was denied. They therefore brought a habeas corpus application and tried to argue that their detention was illegal because it was based on a provision which was no longer constitutional. The Court, despite that, said: You're no longer before us on -- in that case, to be fair, it was on everything. I mean, it wasn't like here, where we're still before you on appeal. But my submission would be that the principle there is the same and that the conviction appeal is final, and the conviction appeal is not before you on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If that is so, your submission would be: We are not in the flow of the case still here because there's been a final judgement on conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Brady will address the next issue. I'll just move out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honours, my colleague Mr. Farrell has already informed you about the grounds of appeal that I'll be addressing on this morning, and there are two of them. One is in relation to the common ground of appeal raised by all three appellants concerning the effect of the dismissal of the cumulative convictions on sentence, and the other is the one that's raised specifically by the appellant Mucic in relation to the third ground of his appellate brief. Now, Your Honours, this morning we have not heard too many arguments directly on the question of the effect of the dismissal of the cumulative convictions on sentence, that is, the sentencing Trial Chamber's dealing with that question. There were some submissions made by Ms. Sinatra on behalf of Landzo, and I'll deal with those, and there were also some tangential submissions made on behalf of all three of the appellants relating to the nature of the proceedings, the proper scope of the proceedings before the second Trial Chamber, which do tangentially relate to this issue. In my arguments, I'd like to flesh out some of the arguments we made in the response brief in order to show you that the focus of this question which is now before you on this issue needs to change, and it's a narrow focus on this question. It's this: Did the second Trial Chamber make an error of law or commit a discernible error in the exercise of its sentencing discretion by failing to reduce the appellants' sentences on their Article 2 convictions on the basis that their Article 3 convictions were dismissed? And as the learned Judge Meron this morning pointed out when he noted paragraph 42 of the second Trial Chamber's reasoning, that paragraph, and paragraphs 34 to 42 that precede it, show, in the Prosecution's position, that it did not make an error. Now, of course, paragraph 42 sets out a summary conclusion as to why the second Trial Chamber thought that the dismissal of the cumulative convictions should have no effect on their sentence for the remaining counts, and, Your Honours, this was after they had engaged in what we say was an entirely appropriate analysis. Moreover, if I could briefly go to that analysis, I'll show Your Honours that it is one that reveals no error. Firstly, and most importantly, following the Appeals Chamber's instructions and the many observations made by the Appeals Chamber on the importance of the totality principle in sentencing, what the second Trial Chamber did was to look at the totality of the appellants' criminal conduct in order to reach a final sentence to reflect the totality of the culpable conduct and overall culpability of the appellants. Now, this morning Mr. Mucic and, if I heard correctly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- both said something to the effect that the second Trial Chamber had no basis, no record upon which it was doing this exercise. But we disagree with that. In fact, apart from the mitigating -- what I would call the up-to-date mitigating evidence, which my colleague Mr. Farrell has dealt with, in fact it did have the full record before it, setting out the full circumstances of the crimes of these three appellants. For Mr. Mucic, the second Trial Chamber goes into a summary of the criminal conduct underlying his Article 2 convictions, and then went on to consider the reasons why his original sentence was considered inadequate by the Appeals Chamber, and then went on to also consider the possible effect of the first Trial Chamber's adverse reference to his failure to testify, and all this in light of the Appeals Chamber's ten-year sentence indication. For Mr. Delic, the same thing. If one looks at the approach of the second Trial Chamber, it summarised the criminal conduct for which he was convicted under the Article 2 and noted that the Appeals Chamber had rejected his claim that his original sentence was excessive, and held that while some reduction would be given in light of the acquittal for one wilful killing, this would be slight in view of the serious offences for which he was convicted. Same analysis done in terms of Landzo. Your Honours, we submit that the appellants haven't shown that in doing so, the second Trial Chamber erred in concluding that the totality of their criminal conduct was not reduced by quashing the cumulative convictions, and that sentences of 15 years for Mr. Landzo, 18 years for Mr. Delic, and 9 years for Mr. Mucic do indeed reflect the application of the totality principle. Now, this totality principle and the application there by the second Trial Chamber shows why some of the arguments which had been put forward by the appellants in their appellants' brief are too simplistic. For example, merely because a defendant stands convicted of fewer offences, his sentence must be reduced. Or because the first Appeals Chamber thought the Article 2 offences were more specific than the Article 3 ones, somehow the overall assessment of his conduct is less. It's also too simplistic to say that a person who is convicted of many crimes should generally receive a higher sentence than one convicted of only one crime. Both of these submissions fail to appreciate this totality principle in sentencing. Now, apart from the totality principle, which was clearly at the forefront of the second Trial Chamber's mind, let's not forget as well that the second Trial Chamber had, in fact, the benefit of the first Trial Chamber's reasoning on this issue by way of the judgement, and this shows that it was more -- that the second Trial Chamber was more than entitled to conclude as it did, in paragraph 42, that the original Trial Chamber specifically had this totality factor in mind in passing the sentences, which clearly would have been the same without the cumulative convictions. Now, we agree that one of the determinative factors when a matter is remitted in this fashion back after dismissal of convictions on appeal may well be the original sentencing Tribunal's intention. We take no issue with that statement raised by two of the appellants. And in fact, the first Appeals Chamber asked the second Trial Chamber to do this. In paragraph 769, when referring to dismissals under Article 3 for Mr. Mucic, the first Appeals Chamber held that this will require that the sentencing consequences be considered by a reconstituted Trial Chamber which will no doubt consider whether the remarks of the original Trial Chamber indicate that there should be no adjustment downwards in the sentence imposed. What we do say is that when they did this review or look at what the first Trial Chamber had done, that the presumption-of-harm test that the appellants say should have been applied actually doesn't apply here. And the reason is this: Because if you look at the first Trial Chamber's judgement, this shows, in several portions of that judgement, that it was aware of the need not to impermissibly cumulatively punish but instead to focus on sentencing for the totality of their criminal conduct. Your Honours, there are several factors which we rely on for this. Firstly, they make -- the first Trial Chamber made several references in its judgement to the question of sentence being dependent upon the particular circumstances of the crime and the role of the accused in it; secondly, the use of concurrent and identical sentences for each of the offenders. Now, while we agree that using concurrent sentences will not of itself prove that the sentencing Tribunal is live to this possibility of cumulative punishment - and indeed this principle was recently upheld in the Kunarac Appeals Chamber decision - that the prejudice is not automatically cured. Your Honours, we submit that a reasonable interpretation of what the first Trial Chamber did shows that it was specifically using this technique of concurrent sentences to avoid cumulative punishment, that this was what it had firmly in its mind, and we read the second Trial Chamber's notation of this in paragraph 34 to support our interpretation of that approach. Finally, Your Honours, the first Trial Chamber also referred to the need to avoid double punishment for the same conduct based on convictions for 7(1) and 7(3), which we submit shows an awareness that the sentence must accurately recognise the gravity of the offences and reflect the totality of the accused's criminal conduct. So even in the situation where there are permissible cumulative convictions, it still must be at the forefront of the Trial Chamber's mind not to punish twice for the same conduct. Clearly, it can punish for the additional element represented by that permissible cumulative conviction, and we would point Your Honours to Your Honours' observations, the Appeals Chamber in this case, Celebici, at paragraph 769. So in summary on this point, Your Honours, we -- and we would like to actually just address the submission made by Ms. Sinatra this morning about the stigma and the problems in cumulative sentencing and the reliance on the dissenting opinion of Judges Hunt and Bennouna. What we say is this: that the Appeals Chamber decision which quashed the Article 3 convictions, that's what removed the stigma could result from the cumulative Article 3 convictions and any potential collateral problems or prejudice relating to early release or subsequent convictions in another jurisdiction. And in remitting the matter back to the second Trial Chamber in this manner for reconsideration, in which they adopted a very careful approach, both totality and looking at the original sentencing Tribunal's intention, this has removed any potential now for impermissible cumulative sentencing, and so for this reason, Your Honour, we would ask Your Honours to dismiss this ground of appeal. Your Honours, before turning to the second ground related to the effect of the first Trial Chamber's adverse comment on Mucic's failure to testify, I'd ask Your Honours if you have any questions on the cumulative convictions and sentencing point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, may I suggest perhaps that it's a narrower issue even than the one you have put forward. Whilst I'm flattered that some of the appellants seem to think that what I and Judge Bennouna said in our dissenting opinion should be the law, on this particular issue, what we said was consistent with the majority decision as to whether or not the Trial Chamber, when they had imposed cumulative convictions, had in fact added to the length of the sentence, and that is the issue which was sent back to the Trial Chamber to determine. So it's a very narrow issue: Was the Trial Chamber wrong, on an appealable basis, in saying that the sentences would clearly have been the same without the cumulative sentences? That's an issue, that's a finding of fact which the appellants have to demonstrate is wrong on an appealable basis, one which no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached, and that is the test which both the majority judgement and the minority judgement posed as the issue for the new Trial Chamber to determine. That's the simple issue, as I see it. Now, I don't think that anything you've said is inconsistent with that, but have you got any problem with that as the issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Your Honour. In fact, that is the issue that we would like to narrow this ground to. And the submissions that we've made go to show why there was no error in that consideration of that issue, because the second Trial Chamber bore in mind the two most fundamental circumstances: the totality of the criminal conduct, as well as the first Trial Chamber's original intent. I would submit -- we would submit that as an abundance of caution, they looked below to what the first Trial Chamber did, and they were satisfied that the intention of that first Trial Chamber could be discerned and that no extra or harsher punishment had been imposed merely by the imposition of a sentence for Article 2 and Article 3 offences for the same underlying conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Gunawardana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Did the acquittal on Article 3 charges in any way weaken the evidence that was available against the Article 2 charges in the proof of the ingredients of the offence of Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand your question correctly, you're asking whether the Article 3 counts were based on the same conduct as the Article 2 counts or the same evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: I'm asking on the impact of the acquittal on Article 3. My question is: Did the acquittal on Article 3 charges weaken the evidence in regard to the proof of the ingredients in respect of Article 2 charges?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: No, it did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I follow up, Ms. Brady, the last question this way: In this case, the first Trial Chamber proceeded on the basis that the sentences, though multiple, were to be concurrent. Is there such a thing as individualisation of sentences, that is to say, that a sentence must be appropriate to the circumstances of the particular conviction in respect of which it is imposed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the thing of individualisation of sentences is that the sentence must be imposed for the totality of the culpable conduct, well, then, we would say yes, that individualisation of sentence is really about meeting -- rendering a sentence which meets the appropriate -- which meets the conduct of the crime, among other things, of course, taking into account mitigating and aggravating circumstances. But if we understand the concept of individualisation of sentences correctly, it's derivative, it's a corollary of the principle of totality, the totality principle in sentencing, and the totality principle gives effect, more or less, to the fact that the sentence will be based on the individual circumstances of both the crime and the offender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put it --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I don't know if that answers Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Partly. Let me put it this way to you: My recollection is that Delic was convicted of the murder of Milosevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And was sentenced to 20 years?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That stands, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: That conviction is upheld, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, is there anything on the record which suggests that imposing that 20-year sentence, in respect of the death of Milosevic, on Delic, the first Trial Chamber took into account his criminal conduct in respect of any other conviction? Or would it be this: Is there something in the record which suggests that if the first Trial Chamber had convicted Delic only on count 3, only on count 3, that the sentence of 20 years which it imposed would have been less?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't think of a specific statement or anything on the record made by the first Trial Chamber which would prove Your Honour's point, but what Your Honour's point may prove is that Trial Chambers, because we have -- we are allowed -- there is a situation where cumulative convictions are permissible, just in the same way as a global sentence may be imposed for a multitude of conduct, it doesn't show that one piece of conduct is raising the stakes, as it were, on consideration of the same conduct on a different count. I'm not sure if that completely makes sense, Your Honour. I think I would have to have some further thought on Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Ms. Brady. That ends your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: On that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The Article 2 charge, of which Judge Shahabuddeen was asking about, was for wilful killing. The Article 3 charge, for which the conviction has now been quashed, is murder. And the issue which I think was being posed to you was: Is there anything in relation to the murder charge which would have increased the sentence for wilful killing?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Not in our submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I thought it was, but I just thought I'd draw your attention to the specific two charges that were laid. And it's the wilful killing one that we are left with instead of the murder one. And was there anything additional in the murder charge, in relation to the proof of the murder charge, that would have increased the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because the conduct was the same, and that's why the cumulative conviction was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you very much, Ms. Brady, for your argument. Let me just start by agreeing with the comments made earlier this morning by Judge Hunt, referring to his opinion in Celebici, jointly with Judge Bennouna, on the real risk of prejudice which is involved in allowing cumulative convictions for the same conduct. May I also point out that of course this particular comment of his which has been adopted by the Appeals Chamber in the Kunarac case. We really must be extremely careful, therefore, in dealing with this question of cumulative convictions, which explains the comments made by my colleagues. In this context, I would like to ask you a question. May I draw your attention to footnote 1458, paragraph 854, page 305, of the appeals judgement. There the Appeals Chamber stated, and I quote: "Because the convictions on the Article 2 counts, based on the same conduct as the quashed Article 3 counts, remain, the adjustment required in relation to the quashing of the convictions may not necessarily be a substantial one." Now, does this language not suggest that some downward adjustment was in fact contemplated by the Appeals Chamber? Could we have your comments on that, Ms. Brady?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. This argument was also put by the appellants that the Appeals Chamber, by remitting -- it shows that it thought that the sentences were decreased, and they point to certain language in the Appeals Chamber judgement to try and illustrate that. Your Honour, there are various references throughout the Appeals Chamber's judgement to what the proper scope -- the mandate of the second Trial Chamber on this issue. In fact, there are some eight or so references to this question. Your Honours, we do realise that that footnote exists, but if one looks at paragraphs 431 and 710 to 712, I think that the clear language of this shows that the Appeals Chamber was setting a clear mandate for the second Trial Chamber. It wasn't making a judgement that the adjustment must occur; it was asking the second Trial Chamber to consider whether an adjustment for the remaining counts was required. Your Honours, in this regard, I also note that the second Trial Chamber dealt specifically with this argument when it was put before them, and in paragraph 39 it called the argument misconceived and that it had misrepresented the Appeal Chamber's meaning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of the time, I'll be very brief on the ground of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, the consensus is that you may proceed, on the understanding that you will, as usual, observe the principles of brevity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I always try to. Your Honour, this question concerns the submissions made by Mucic that breach of the principle that no adverse use can be made of the accused's exercise of his right not to testify requires a substantial reduction of his sentencing, and they also advert to the question: Why the difference in treatment between the second Trial Chamber's approach to this error and their approach to the cumulative conviction one. Mr. Morrison directly, and Mr. Moran, asked why this difference was in existence. It's because of this: The first Trial Chamber's remark about his failure to give evidence not only disclosed an error, but left open the real possibility that it was treated as an aggravating factor on sentence. So therefore, the remit, or the question before the sentencing -- the second Trial Chamber was: How much of a reduction? Does this affect the final sentence that we impose? On the other hand, when dealing with cumulative convictions under Article 2 and 3, it was not that the Appeals Chamber said this was an error which led to impermissibly cumulatively punish. That was the question, the very question, for the second Trial Chamber. So that explains the difference in approach. As for the principle itself and whether or not it's so fundamental as to require a fundamental breach, we have already asserted this in our brief, and our position is that this breach is not so fundamental that the second Trial Chamber made an error by not giving it a substantial reduction. We say that the reliance on US case-law in this instance is somewhat misplaced. Firstly, as Your Honours well know, this Court doesn't do a wholesale incorporation of the laws of any one particular country into its jurisprudence. Secondly, when the Appeals Chamber itself upheld that there had been a breach of the principle, it canvassed many jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom and the European Court of Human Rights, which basically showed that in many jurisdictions this principle is being watered down. So from that we -- it's difficult to get into an argument based on a sort of relativity of rights, but we submit that this right is not of such fundamental importance as to require a substantial reduction. And in terms of the cases provided by Mr. Mucic's counsel, in particular, the one that he has provided to us yesterday, the Mitchell case, that case, even if it does stand for the proposition that someone would get a substantial reduction in sentence for such an error is distinguishable from the case at hand. In the Mitchell case, a factual adverse inference as to the amount of drugs supplied by a defendant was drawn from an accused person's silence, and this quantum of drugs had direct implications for the sentence of this person. In effect, it was completing an element of the crime, although it was at the stage of a plea. Whereas for Mr. Mucic, here the adverse comment, if any, was to treat it as an aggravating factor in consideration of an appropriate sentence for what had already been established as his criminal conduct. In brief, Your Honours, in view of the seriousness of Mr. Mucic's crimes and his role, we submit that there was no error, that the second Trial Chamber did not venture outside of its scope of its discretionary sentencing framework by imposing a nine-year sentence for his crimes, and for this reason we ask that you dismiss this ground. Thank you, Your Honours. If you have any questions on that issue, I'd be happy to take them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, there are no questions from the Bench. We will suspend now for 15 minutes and then we will return and hopefully conclude, if we can, with the cooperation of our interpreters, if they are so disposed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ready, Mr. Carmona?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that you will finish within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Ten minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That will enable us to keep time. We want to balance it fairly between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I will be handling two particular grounds of Delic. This is in relation to grounds 6 and 7. However, there is a need, in fact, to respond to some arguments raised by my learned colleagues on the other side in relation to two particular issues. My learned friend on the other side has indicated that there is a witness that recognised a different voice. I wish to say very categorically that this, in fact, was the subject of a motion by the Defence to open review of proceedings, where the statement was exhibited. And in that decision on the motion for review on the 20th of April, 2002, it was dismissed. Any attempt through the proverbial back door to reconsider or reassess this particular fact must not be encouraged or endorsed. That door must not only be shut, it must be locked. Additionally, in relation to my learned friend Moran on the other side, he indicated a lack of awareness in relation to the Kunarac judgement. In that particular motion for review, the decision, the learned Appeals Chamber had mentioned very categorically that the Appeals Chamber will not intervene, at paragraph 15, because of an attorney's -- of one attorney adopting one position or in hindsight effecting an error. It is only when the decision made was of such a nature in the circumstances of the case as to have led to a miscarriage of justice. When one looks at the nature of the cross-examination in relation to all of those witnesses, when one looks at the motion to dismissal, when one looks at the final brief, counsel quite competently attacked the quality of the evidence led by the Prosecution and, therefore, in fact, notwithstanding his being fully au courant with the tenets of that particular decision that no miscarriage resulted. If I may now move on to the particular ground of appeal. The first is that the first Trial Chamber erred by importing the words "if any" into their consideration of adjustment of sentence in respect of Delic's acquittal on counts 1 and 2. This, very critically, is an area of new interpretation, and I think in this regard I wish to quote, in part but in extenso, a particular judgement, Stoddardt, of 1909, 2 Criminal Appeal Reports, which is in our brief, by Lord Chief Justice Alverstone, where he says, in relation to the issue of reviewing summing-ups, he says: "This Court does not sit to consider whether this or that phrase was the best that might have been chosen, or whether a direction which has been attacked must have been fuller or more conveniently expressed, or whether other topics which might have been dealt with on other occasions should be introduced. The Court sits here to administer justice and to deal with valid objections to matters which may have led to a miscarriage of justice." It is the position of the Prosecution that notwithstanding the input, if any, that there is no miscarriage of justice and that in fact there is no prejudice to, in fact, the appellant. On this issue of general awareness as to what the Trial Chamber, the constituted Trial Chamber, saw its role and its mandate as, it is important to appreciate that there was a motion for clarification, a joint motion, which the appellants made or filed in relation to determining what ought -- the scope of the briefs ought to be and what is the scope of the oral hearing. In that particular decision, the Trial Chamber very categorically said that in fact they would be dealing in relation to Delic but what adjustment, if any, should be made to the sentence of Hazim Delic after the Appeals Chamber quashed his conviction in relation to count 1 and 2. It is submitted that this decision not to raise the matter again with the Trial Chamber is an indication that the appellant was in agreement with the interpretation given to the particular order and made the submissions accordingly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Certainly. He was not, therefore, prejudiced in the conduct of his submissions as reflected in the scope and breadth of his arguments. Additionally, one should realise a note in paragraph 32 of the second Trial Chamber's ruling in dealing with ancillary issues that are dismissed in relation to parole, commutation of sentence and re-allocation. It said that these issues are wholly irrelevant to the issue remitted before it, namely, adjustment of sentence in light of the various acquittals. The Trial Chamber was -- indeed stated very matter of factly what its mandate was. In other words, what we need to determine is what was the object and purpose of the order, and this must be done from the position of an intelligent interpretation of that particular order.
