When the Chamber, at paragraph 712, said that it would be convenient - rather, 713 - said that it would be convenient, when the matter is remitted, for the new Trial Chamber also to consider what adjustment should be made, this was made in the context of what went before. Also, obviously would have meant in like manner. Apart from that, when one looks from a -- strictly from a sense of nomenclature, when one considers what is meant by considering, it merely means -- it means evaluating the merits and demerits of the particular position. In that regard, it is the submission of, in fact, the Prosecution that the submission of, in fact -- the submission of the appellant Delic is an exercise, an adventure in technicality, and this, in fact, type of technicality was addressed in Barayagwiza by the learned Judge Shahabuddeen, who indicated that whether a party - and this is in my brief - was or was not subject to an unfair procedure is a matter of substance, not technicality. And this is borne out by the fact that the appellant attorney, in submission, emphasised, throughout the tenor of his address, that in fact what he was concerned with is substance and not form. It is ironic that he is now attacking form. When one looks at the entire ambit of the order, it was obvious that the discretion in relation to the whole issue of sentence was, in fact, left with that reconstituted Trial Chamber within the specific confines. And insofar as the appellant has not been able to show that he was prejudiced in any way, this particular ground of appeal must fail. In any event, when one considers that in the disposition reference is made to original sentences in the context of the issue of a judgement, it may well be that in fact that the Appeals Chamber was in fact putting on an inquiry that original sentences were being reviewed and would be readjusted. So, Your Honours, it is important to appreciate that in dealing with this particular ground of appeal, that we must not adopt a microscopic approach to an assessment of a ruling. And this is borne out by the fact that recently, in the case of -- in the recent decision of Kunarac that was given on the 12th of June, 2002, where in fact the particular Appeals Chamber had to deal with an alleged omission with regard to credit for time served. In that particular -- those particular paragraphs, paragraphs 363 to 365, the Court resorted to looking at the record in determining whether, in fact, there was indeed an error. In this particular instance, we are on a better footing. The Appeals Chamber can look not only at the record but at the actual judgement in itself, contextually and in relation to what is the spirit and object of that disposition. My learned friend on the other side, at paragraph 57 of his brief, appears to be making a ground, putting forward a position that in part appears incomprehensible. But if he's intimating that he was misled and that his arguments did not establish -- could have been better placed, he has not shown how the interpretation left him uncertain as to the nature of the exercise. It is trite that the appellate process is not intended to fill a lacuna, a trial, or to correct a mistaken strategy at trial. If I may now move on to the second aspect of the particular ground dealing with the adjustment of the Delic's sentence in relation to the quashing of his convictions in count 1 and 2. It is important to note initially that as much as, in fact, it has been put forward that counts 1 and 2 were quashed, it represents one criminal conduct. It is important to note that the appellant concedes that Delic's overall sentence cannot be less than 15 years, which is the length of the next most serious crime he received in relation to the counts of torture by way of rape. Again I have to be careful in indicating to the Court that this argument with regard to 15 years must not be seen as a back-door attempt or should not be seen or in fact should be -- should, in fact, be -- that the Appeals Chamber should be critical of viewing this as a possible attempt on the part of the appellant to revisit the issue of the argument in relation to maximum sentences in the former Yugoslavia. However, by insisting on a 15-year maximum, what, in fact, the appellant has done is illustrate quite succinctly that a discretion exercised by the reconstituted Trial Chamber was proper and reasonable when one considers that a particular sentence they gave was, in fact, 18 years. I will not, for purposes of economy, go into the actual offences for which, in fact, he was convicted, apart from indicating that in paragraph 715 they are outlined, and more specifically that they were termed "rather sadistic" and described in very derogatory terms by the Trial Chamber in the context of criminal culpability. I submit finally that when one considers the sentence, that the particular dismissal in no way vitiated the inherent criminal conduct of this appellant. And insofar as we can look at the authority of Musema, which indicates that an Appeals Chamber has -- that a Trial Chamber has a discretion -- and this was endorsed by Musema, in Musema, for genocide. One of the rapes was, in fact, dismissed, yet the Court found that life imprisonment was the appropriate sentence. In this particular case, notwithstanding the dismissal of that particular count, the Court was of the view that he did deserve, in fact, a certain diminution and gave it to him in the form of two years. It is the submission of the Prosecution, and I say this because, in fact, I have -- I made a promise to the Appeals Chamber that I would in fact take ten minutes, I stand by the arguments that we have presented in our appeal brief, and we submit, in fact, that the appellant has not shown that he was in any way prejudiced by the fact that the -- by the Appeals Chamber indicating omitting the word "any," "in any," and also in relation to the dismissal of those two -- of those two counts in the indictment. Essentially, Your Honours, these are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question from Judge Gunawardana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: When you said criminal conduct of the accused, did you mean that the same ingredients go to prove both the offences under Article 2 and Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm saying, for example, these two offences represent two distinct offences. They were two distinct offences, and, therefore, they attracted the corresponding penalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Under penalty, the ingredients of one offence match the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed, under the cumulative conviction concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Will it necessarily result in the gravity of the conviction under 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: What is important to note is that in fact in relation to the murder of Milosevic, the appellant, in fact, received 15 years. Yes, 15 years. Sorry, 20 years. So that as much as, in fact, for example, they represent two distinct offences and as much as, in fact, they fall under the rubric of cumulative convictions, it is the submission that it wouldn't have affected the final sentence. And if, in fact, it did, Your Honours, as -- if the Court was of the view that, in fact, it did result in a particular diminution, a particular accounting, they did give it to him in the form of two years. And this particular exercisable discretion was found to be quite reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: But the diminution of conviction was the same as the conviction under 2, Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: The diminution under Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, what in fact transpired is that the particular appellant was charged with two killings and one particular killing, in fact, he was found not guilty of. This is no relation to Gotovac. The Court was of the view that there may be a need to readjust the particular sentence in the context of that particular finding and to send the particular matter back to be considered by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber, in fact, took that into consideration and in so doing decided, for example, that -- that two years was the type of accounting he would in fact have received, and they did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Carmona. And this is just to clear my own mind on a proposition which I believe you made. You were talking of the dismissal of the motion for the production of additional evidence. I'm not clear whether your submission was to the effect that the dismissal of that motion operated to preclude the appellants from arguing that on the basis of the record as it otherwise stood, the sufficiency of evidence principle was not satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed, My Lord, Your Worship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's your proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed, yes. That we are, in fact, saying basically that -- yes. In we, in fact, saying that as much as, in fact, the particular motion in fact dismissed the particular attempt to lead additional evidence, if I may say it, that in any event, in fact, the Appeals Chamber was of the view that it did not raise any additional argument to warrant an additional review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is a different position today. All right. I'll try and understand that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does that conclude the case for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then, I return to the appellants. You have 15 minutes in which to reply. Who is going to do this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're going to break it up, and I have just a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have a few short matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that some flexibility is needed, so we will overstep the 15 minutes a little but not too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge, as the last thing you were questioning the Prosecution about on that order from the Trial Chamber, there's a case from my jurisdiction I think should be read by all lawyers, and it stands for the proposition that when a Judge makes a decision, if you don't like the decision, you obey what the Judge says and then you appeal it later. And that's exactly what we did. The Trial Chamber made a decision. We respected the Trial Chamber's decision, and we're appealing it later. If that's the wrong thing to do, I'd like to know of something different that wouldn't be contemptuous adventures in technicality. When he read that quote from you, Judge Shahabuddeen, it reminded me of a Judge I used to practice before named John Onion. And Judge Onion used to say, "There is no such thing as a technicality. It's either the law or it's not." And things are either the law or they're not. Judge, this Tribunal, and I think all courts, don't sentence crimes. You sentence people who are convicted of committing crimes. And there's a big difference. In this case, what we asked to do -- what my client asked to do at the second Appeals Chamber -- or second Trial Chamber at resentencing was to present some evidence in mitigation, which could have been done in writing, which in fact was presented in writing and was rejected, and he wanted the opportunity to stand up in front of those Judges and say he has thought about what he was charged with, he has thought about what occurred in the former Yugoslavia and to show remorse for the acts that he committed. That's all we asked. Burden of proof. The -- at least as to Delic, this case was sent back for two reasons, and at this point I'll just discuss the reassessment for cumulative sentencing. There is no evidence in the record one way or the other as to whether that affected the judgement of the original Trial Chamber. There's no way to know. Short of picking up the telephone and calling the original members of the Trial Chamber, we'll never know whether that affected them. The question is: Was it error? Yes, this Trial Chamber has said it was error. And the next question is: If it's error, should the Defence, the victim of the error, have to prove that he was harmed, or should the person who benefited from the error, the Prosecution, have to prove that the defendant was not harmed? I submit to you that the beneficiary of an error should be required to prove lack of harm. Two other things and then I'll sit down. There was a question about a final judgement. When I used words "final judgement" -- and a lot of us come from the same legal tradition but we speak a slightly different language, when I say the words "final judgement," what I mean is a judgement that disposes of all parties, all issues, and there is nothing left for any Court to do except put the judgement into effect. I think that is what's contemplated by both Rule 92 ter and Rule 117, that there would be one judgement, not a separate judgement for sentencing and a separate judgement for conviction. And that judgement is final, in my view, when all of the issues that were in that litigation have been finally decided, all of the parties have been finally decided and disposed of and there is nothing for the Chamber to do or for the Tribunal to do except execute the judgement. Under that view, there is no final judgement in Celebici as to anything. There are judgements, but there is no final judgement. And the last thing is, Judge, even under the Rule 115 cases, as I understand them, if there is a pure miscarriage of justice, this Chamber will consider new evidence. And I'm asking you to consider essentially new arguments. I would submit to the Appeals Chamber that a wrongful conviction, by definition, is a miscarriage of justice, and I would submit to the Appeals Chamber that if a conviction will not withstand a sufficiency of the evidence review, under our law it's a wrongful conviction and would be a miscarriage of justice. Unless the Chamber has some questions, I'll let my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. Moran. Would any counsel for the other appellants wish to speak? We still have a few minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Morrison and I both have some brief submissions to make in rebuttal. I will go further since I'm standing. My rebuttal submission deals with the cumulative convictions issue. The Prosecutor has relied on and discussed today paragraph 42 of the new Trial Chamber's judgement, and to go along with something that Mr. Moran said, it is difficult if not impossible to peer inside the minds of those original Judges and see what they have determined. And by that I just read one sentence in paragraph 42. Actually, two sentences: "In the case of the three accused, the totality of their criminal conduct has not been reduced by reason of the quashing of the cumulative convictions." There's no citation or anything in the record or anything that's referred to. "The original Trial Chamber specifically had this factor in mind in passing the sentences which clearly would have been the same without the cumulative convictions." Again, no citations to the record. And it begs the question: How do you know that the original Trial Chamber specifically had this factor in mind? And that's problematic for us on the cumulative conviction issue. The other portion of that, Your Honours, is that in the original Appeals Chamber's decision, impact of the cumulative convictions on sentencing at paragraph 431, the sentence reads: "The Appeals Chamber acknowledges that if the Trial Chamber had not imposed double convictions, a different outcome in terms of the length and manner of sentencing might have resulted." And note that the language is "sentencing," not "adjustment." Because this is a matter that lies within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, this Chamber remits the issue of sentencing, not adjustment, to a Trial Chamber to be designated by the President of the Tribunal. And that, to me, indicates an intent, at least, through that paragraph 431 that there will be a sentencing. Not necessarily a hearing, but at least some kind of evidence to bring the new Trial Chamber up to speed on the facts and circumstances of each particular accused at that stage in time in their lives. Those, Your Honours, are my submissions unless there are any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll leave the balance to Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honours, two very brief matters. Ms. Brady in her reply espoused the test of a real risk of prejudice. In Mr. Mucic's case there isn't a risk of prejudice. The prejudice is palpable and is demonstrated by the wording in the original Trial Chamber's judgement and in the context not only of the wording but of the other criticisms they make of him. And so we say it is not a question simply of redressing a risk, redressing an actual prejudice, not merely to compensate Mr. Mucic but also to bring the system into public confidence. The second point she makes by analysis with what was ascribed to as the watering down of the right to silence in other jurisdictions is that in the Trial Chamber's original judgement in this case, and the Appeals Chamber's original judgement in the case the right to silence was defined as absolute. If the Prosecution are now seeking to amend that from being absolute to conditional, then a proper basis for such a radical change of jurisprudence would have to be made and no such basis has been made or even alluded to in these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. The Bench has been -- You desire to speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just have one or two things, if I may, on behalf of Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the ultimate issue in this appeal on the jurisdictional ground is really a very simple one, and that is whether the Tribunal will follow its own Statute and Rules. The Prosecution suggests that Article 25(2) can be interpreted purposively because it is in some way ambiguous, and they pray in aid the contention that Article 25(2) does not specifically, for example, provide a right of appeal against sentence. But what Article 25(2) clearly does is to give the Appeals Chamber the power and the duty to affirm, reverse, or revise the decisions taken by the Trial Chambers. Sentencing is a decision taken by the Trial Chambers, and that follows clearly from the wording of the Rule. In this instance, the interpretation of Article 25(2) as being ambiguous sets up a conflict between that Rule -- or that Article and Article 24, because the sentencing law of this Tribunal is that under Article 24, the individual circumstances of the accused should be taken into account when sentencing, and Rule 101(B) makes that mandatory. Now, what happened in this case was that the second Trial Chamber found itself in a position where it was called upon to sentence the appellants without complying with these mandatory provisions, and we say that that's a matter of law and that it's wrong. And we don't -- and, Your Honours, when we used in our brief the expression "per in curiam," we don't intend to be critical of the first Appeals Chamber for this. The matter wasn't raised. It wasn't argued, and it was understandable that such an order might be made. But we've had the opportunity now to look at it in the light of the Articles and the Rules. Now, the Prosecution continues to say, well, Tadic provides authority for remitting on a discrete issue. Your Honours, if you will look at the portions from Tadic that we've cited, you will see that what happened there was effectively and could be described as a new trial according to law. That's all these appellants want. They -- And the final point, addressing the matter that has been raised: Well, could the appellants have introduced new evidence before the first Appeals Chamber relevant to sentence? Apparently, this is the practice in some jurisdictions. I have consulted with my learned friends on the Defence side, and I think, modestly, we have between us a good number of years both in England and the United States and we have never collectively known a case where that has been done. We have known cases where the Court of Appeal has said that such evidence is inappropriate because it's irrelevant. The issue before the Appeals Chamber is that did the sentencing court get it right or not at the time. Now, if such a rule is introduced, and it may be that the Appeals Chamber feels that that rule has merit, that the appellant should introduce new evidence, we feel we should make the Appeals Chamber aware that the inevitable result of this will be an application under Rule 115 to admit additional evidence in any future case in which there is an appeal against sentence. It will become the automatic practice of the Tribunal. Under the existing law, we would submit that that was not required and indeed would have been inappropriate. So for those reasons, Your Honours, unless you have any questions, those are my submissions in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, I don't have a question, but I do have a warning. It could never be admissible under 115 because it's not a rehearing. You may be able to, as Mr. Farrell conceded, put in material which is relevant to a resentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You would have to do that under some Rule, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, you don't. A Trial Chamber, under the Rules -- I'm sorry. Any Chamber, including the Appeals Chamber, can receive evidence which is relevant to the issue which it has to determine. It sounds as if you've been in a civil law system all your life and I know that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So I am absolutely astounded that you would put that submission. But it is not under 115. It would be evidence which is relevant to the resentencing. And as Mr. Farrell has suggested, it would be in relation to a very limited number of issues that could be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in a way I'm glad to hear that because clearly it is material that ordinarily should be before a sentencing Court. My point is that under the Rules as now established, it appears to be the case that when we come to the Appeals Chamber, the -- what the Appeals Chamber is going to do to affirm, reverse, or revise the decisions taken by the Trial Chamber. And so our position was that in that case, the evidence should be relevant to the situation as it was before the Trial Chamber, which is the basis of the appeal. All I'm saying to the Court, with the greatest of respect, is that if this is to be the Rule, then of course under whatever Rule, it will become automatic for appellants to introduce this kind of evidence in every appeal against sentence, and we don't feel that that has been the law of the Tribunal hitherto, but clearly it would be open to the Tribunal to adopt a Rule to that effect. Unless the Court has any other questions. I'm much obliged, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, may I wrap it up by putting to you my impression of the case on whole? That is that the appellants concede that there could be what you have referred to as a discrete remit but that a new Trial Chamber was obliged to hold a trial on issues relevant to the remit. Was that your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You may be seated. Well, then, that concludes the hearing, and the Appeals Chamber will reserve its judgement in the normal way. You will be notified of the progress of events. Thank you. The Court is adjourned.
